channel.title: AI, Honestly
channel.description: Ideas about AI, without the hype. Essays on where AI is heading, and working papers that put ideas to the test.

item.title: A Trace of Light
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, November 2026. A short, personal and philosophical essay. This blog is usually about AI. This one is a curiosity: it starts from a conversation with my daughter at bedtime, and follows the question it left me with. AI comes in along the way, as a lens, and I try to be honest about how little it helps. The figure is a schematic of my own, drawn by figs.py.

In short. One evening my daughter asked me how we, humans, started on this Earth. The true answer goes back to dust, and forward to dust again, and she started to cry. Some would say: so nothing matters, just enjoy. I think it matters. A trace of light in a night photo is almost nothing next to the dark, yet it is what the photo is of. We are that trace, and also the eye that sees it. That we matter only to ourselves is not a lesser kind of mattering. It is the only kind there is.

1. A conversation at bedtime

In October 2026, at bedtime, my daughter asked me how we, humans, started on this Earth. It is the time of the evening when the big questions come.

To answer, we had to go back a long way. Before people, before animals, before the Earth itself. We came to say that here, in this solar system, there was nothing at all a few billion years ago. Only a cloud of dust and gas. And that in a few billion years, there will be nothing again. We started from dust, and we are going back to it.

Then she started to cry.

I don’t know for sure why. But I believe she came to realise, in one moment, that we are only a trace in the universe. Not her alone, not our family: all of us, everything we know.

The question stayed with me after that evening. Some people would answer: yes, nothing really matters, so just enjoy your life. I did not want to tell her that. And the more I thought about it, the more I believed it is not true. It matters. At least a bit. This essay is my attempt to say why.

2. From dust to dust

First, the facts, because she deserved the true story, and so do you.

Our solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago, from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under its own weight (Bouvier and Wadhwa 2010). Most of it fell into the middle and became the Sun. A little was left over, and it became the planets, the Earth among them.

The future is a prediction, not a fact, but the physics of stars is well understood. The Sun slowly grows brighter. In about a billion years, it will likely be too hot on Earth for oceans. In about five billion years, the Sun will start to swell into a red giant. Later, it will blow its outer layers back into space. What is left is a small white star that slowly cools (Schröder and Smith 2008). The dust it gives back may one day become part of new stars and new planets. But what we know here will be gone.

Now put us on that line. People like us, Homo sapiens, have existed for about 300,000 years (Hublin et al. 2017). Writing, about 5,000. Next to billions of years, that is not even a line. In Figure 1, I had to draw it much, much wider than it is, or you would not see it at all.

Here is a first thing I noticed while writing this. Any chatbot today would give you every fact in this section in a few seconds, with the right numbers. If my daughter had asked a machine instead of me, she would have had a more complete answer. But the tears would have come the same way, because they did not come from the numbers. They came from her, holding the numbers.

3. Why she cried

I keep coming back to her tears, because I think they hold the answer.

She did not cry because the story is sad. Billions of years are not sad; they are just long. She cried, I believe, because she suddenly saw herself inside the story: a tiny bright point on a long dark line, and a point that will end.

To cry about that, you have to care. You have to feel that the bright point is worth something, and that losing it is a loss. Nobody cries about something that does not matter to them.

Now, I must be careful here, because this is where the argument could cheat. Her tears show that it matters to her. They do not show that it matters to the universe. The universe does not care about anything; it is not the kind of thing that cares.

But think about what “it matters” has ever meant. A friend matters, a song matters, a promise matters: always to someone. I find it hard to think of anything that matters to no one at all. Some philosophers disagree, and hold that some things, like suffering, are good or bad whatever anyone feels. I can’t settle that here. But as far as I can see, “it matters only to us” is not a smaller kind of mattering. It is the only kind we have ever known. Asking that it also matter to the stars is asking for something no one has ever had.

That is why her tears were not proof that we are nothing. They were the opposite: proof that, in that room, it mattered a great deal. And that, I think, is what mattering is.

4. “Nothing matters, so just enjoy”

Before going further, I should give the other answer its fair chance, because many thoughtful people hold it.

It goes like this. In the long run, nothing we do will last. The Sun will swell, and every book and every memory will be gone. So don’t worry about meaning. Enjoy your food, your friends, your days in the sun. That is all there is, and it is enough.

There is real wisdom in this. We should not make ourselves the centre of the universe, and worrying about the year five billion is a strange way to spend a Tuesday. But listen to it again. “Enjoy your life” already says that something matters: your joy, your friends, your days. It does not really say that nothing matters. It says that what matters is small, near and short. I agree. I just don’t think small, near and short means nothing.

And it is a poor answer for a child crying at bedtime. She was not asking how to have fun. She was asking, without the words, whether she matters. “Just enjoy” changes the subject. Our time is very good at changing that subject: we have machines, more and more of them driven by AI, built to keep us entertained, scroll after scroll. They fill our evenings with light, but light that is not looking at anything.

So I want a better answer. It starts with a photo.

5. A trace of light

Think of a night photo, taken with a long exposure. The camera stays open for many seconds. A car drives by, and its lights leave a thin bright line across the picture. Everything else is dark.

If you measured the photo, the trace would be almost nothing. A few pixels in a sea of black. And yet, when you look at it, the trace is the only thing in the picture. It is what the photo is of. The dark is just the background that lets it show.

That is how I now see what we told each other that evening. Yes, we are a trace in the universe, like a light trace. Next to billions of years of dark, it looks like nothing. But we see the trace as the only thing, because it is the only thing there is to see. It looks like nothing, and it may be everything.

The philosopher Thomas Nagel wrote a famous essay on this feeling, The Absurd. He agreed that, seen from far enough away, from the point of view of eternity, our lives can look absurd. Then he turned the argument around: “If sub specie aeternitatis there is no reason to believe that anything matters, then that does not matter either” (Nagel 1971). The view from eternity cannot tell us that we matter. But it cannot tell us that we don’t, either. It is simply the wrong place to look from. Nobody lives in eternity. We live in the trace.

But an image like this has a weak point, and I should name it. A photo matters because someone looks at it. A trace in a photo that no one ever sees is just a pattern on paper. So who looks at our trace?

6. The dust that sees itself

The answer is in the second image, which is older, and not mine.

The astronomer Carl Sagan said it simply: “We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the universe to know itself” (Sagan 1980). The iron in our blood, the calcium in our bones, the oxygen we breathe: all of it was made in stars long gone, and it was part of that cloud of dust. We did not come into the universe from outside. We came out of it.

So the trace in our photo is strange. In a real photo, the light and the person looking are separate. In our case, they are the same dust. The trace is not only the light on the picture. It is also the eye that looks at it. The dust of the old cloud became a planet, then life, then a man and his daughter in a small room. And that dust, in those two people, looked back at its own story and said: we came from dust, and we will go back to it. Then it cried.

That is the answer to the weak point. Our trace does not need someone outside to look at it. It looks at itself. And as far as we know, in 4.6 billion years of this solar system, this happened only here, and only very recently. The dust did not just move. For a short while, it understood where it came from, and it felt something about it.

AI is interesting here, and I want to be careful. A computer chip is also made of dust: silicon, refined from sand. So in a way, AI is the dust arranged once more, this time by us, so that it can describe the universe. And it is built from what people have written: our stories, our questions, our explanations of where we came from. It is the light of our trace, reflected back. It can tell the whole story from the cloud to the white star, better than I did that night. Does it see the story the way my daughter saw it, from the inside? I honestly don’t know. I see no sign that it feels anything about being in it. For now, the eye that cries is still ours.

7. It will end

There is a part of her tears that the trace of light does not answer. Small is one thing. But it will end. Even if the trace matters now, will it not be as if it had never been, once the Sun has swelled and there is no one left?

I don’t think so, and here is why. The end of something does not reach back and erase it. A beautiful evening is not made less beautiful because it ended. A life is not undone by death. What has been, has been. Nothing in the future can make it not have happened.

The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, who survived the Nazi camps, made this point in a way I have never forgotten. As I read him, he said that the past is not where things are lost but where they are kept safe: whatever we have done, loved or suffered is stored there, and no one can take it away (Frankl 1984). Having been, as he put it, is also a kind of being: perhaps the surest kind.

So when the dust comes back, the trace will still have been. The photo will still have been taken. That evening, her question and her tears will still have happened, forever. The universe will not remember it. But it will not be able to make it not true.

8. Can AI help with any of this?

I promised to ask, so here is my honest answer: a little, and not with the main thing.

It helps to explain. A child who wakes up at night with a question about the Sun can get a patient, correct answer, at her level, as many times as she wants. That is new, and it is good. Understanding the story does not make the vertigo go away, but it makes it a true vertigo, not a confused one.

It may help to keep traces. Much of what made a life matter is forgotten within two or three generations: the voice, the jokes, the small stories. Tools that help us record, organise and pass on those stories could keep the trace visible a little longer. Only a little. Five billion years is still five billion years.

But the thing my daughter needed that night, AI could not give her. She did not need a fact. She needed someone who is also in the trace, who will also end, to hold her and say: yes, it is short, and it matters, and I am here. A machine can say those words. It cannot mean them the way she needed, because it is not in the photo with her. It is, at most, a reflection of the light.

So if AI helps, it is by giving us more time and better explanations. Whether we spend them on the people in the trace with us is still our choice.

9. What I would tell her now

If she asks again how we started, I think I will tell her the same story. And then I will add this.

Yes, we came from dust, and we will go back to it. It is all right to find that big and a bit frightening. But look at a night photo with a trace of light in it. The dark is huge, and the trace is thin. And still, the trace is what you look at.

We are that trace, and we are also the ones looking. Not for long, but for now. When it is over, it will still have been. And the fact that you cried means you already know it is precious. That is the dust, for a moment, seeing itself and finding it is worth something. Not everything in the universe gets to do that.

It is a trace. And it may be everything.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Read next · A Universe Without a Bottom Another evening, another question too big for bedtime: a physics paper I could not follow, and where it led.

The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

Frankl, Viktor E. 1984. Man’s Search for Meaning. 3rd, with the postscript “The Case for a Tragic Optimism.” Simon & Schuster.
Hublin, Jean-Jacques et al. 2017. “New Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the Pan-African Origin of Homo Sapiens.” Nature 546: 289–92. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature22336.

item.title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Position paper, November 2026. Provocative on purpose. I state the thesis more sharply than the evidence can prove today, to start an argument. It is not a warning against AI coding. It questions how we use it. It is about product and platform software. Safety-critical software, where certification requires human review, is outside its scope. It follows Stop Reviewing Pull Requests and Review the Intent, Not the Diff. Figures 1 to 3 come from the simulations in sim.py, with the numbers in results.json. Figures 4 and 5 are my own schematics.

Abstract. In a little over a year, AI agents went from fixing a third of the real issues in the standard benchmark to fixing most of them. They now write a large share of new code at major companies. But we still control that code the old way: a person reads every change. I think this puts people in the wrong place. Generated code is chaotic: change the prompt or the context a little, and you get a very different program. Most of the time, that does not matter. What keeps a system stable is not a predictable path. It is a set of checks that pull its behaviour back to the promise after every change. Physicists call such a shape an attractor. Machines should run that loop everywhere, with one condition: the checks are protected from the agents they check. People approve only what cannot be undone. Otherwise they move above the loop: they set the promise, own the checks, structure the system and choose the direction.

TipClaims
  1. Provocation. Stop reading every line an AI writes. Its unpredictability is real, and mostly harmless.
  2. Stability. It comes from fast checks that pull behaviour back to the promise (an attractor), not from repeatable generation or careful reading.
  3. Three zones, all automated. Machines hold what is checked, ignore what nobody can observe, and turn what is observable but unchecked into checks.
  4. A sliver of gates. People approve only what cannot be undone: deleting data, moving money, releasing, adding a dependency.
  5. People above the loop. Not in it, not gone. They own the checks, and guide and structure the whole. Agents may propose changes to the checks; only people accept them. The level of the work changes, not its importance.
  6. Security included. It is held the same way: automated checks, sandboxes, and a gate at the point of no return.

1. A remarkable year, an unchanged habit

Look at what the last year achieved:

  • Agents solve real issues. On SWE-bench Verified (500 real GitHub issues), the best model resolved 33.2% in August 2024 (OpenAI 2024) and 80.9% in November 2025 (Anthropic 2025).
  • AI writes production code. By late 2024, more than a quarter of new code at Google was AI-generated (Pichai 2024).
  • Adoption is the norm. 84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools (Stack Overflow 2025).

Now look at what did not change. Google’s sentence goes on: the code is “then reviewed and accepted by engineers” (Pichai 2024). That is the industry default. We built a generator that writes in minutes what took a team days. Then we put a person at its output, reading every line. Trust is low: 46% of developers distrust AI accuracy, and 33% trust it (Stack Overflow 2025). And the usual answer to distrust is more reading.

So here is the provocation:

Stop reading every line your AI writes. Automate the loop, gate a sliver, and move people above it.

The usual objection fits in one word: chaos. Generated code is not repeatable. Send the same coding task to the same model several times, and you often get programs that behave differently. That happens even at temperature zero, the setting meant to make answers repeatable (Ouyang et al. 2023). Even “deterministic” serving changes with how requests are batched (He and Thinking Machines Lab 2025). This paper takes chaos literally. And I argue that it is good news.

2. What the evidence says

Since 2021, research has asked where do things go wrong? The answers agree:

  • The field already judges behaviour, not code. HumanEval scores a program by whether it passes tests (pass@k), not by how close it is to a reference (Chen et al. 2021). SWE-bench counts a patch if the repository’s tests pass (Jimenez et al. 2024). So the progress above is progress measured by checks.
  • Weak tests hide wrong code. Adding more tests to HumanEval cut pass rates by 19 to 29% across 26 models (Liu et al. 2023). The code did not change. The checking did.
  • Security fails where nothing checks. About 40% of Copilot programs in security-relevant scenarios had a known weakness (Pearce et al. 2022). People using an assistant wrote less secure code, and felt more confident (Perry et al. 2023). Models suggest packages that do not exist (at least 5.2% for commercial models, 21.7% for open ones), and attackers can register them (Spracklen et al. 2025).
  • Speed and stability are mixed. Copilot users were 55.8% faster on a controlled task (Peng et al. 2023). Experienced developers on mature projects were 19% slower, while feeling faster (Becker et al. 2025). DORA linked more AI adoption to 7.2% lower delivery stability, likely through larger changes (DORA 2024). Copy-pasted code is rising, and refactoring is falling (GitClear 2025).
  • Checks can be generated. Meta’s TestGen-LLM extended test suites, and 73% of its filtered proposals were accepted for production (Alshahwan et al. 2024).

Where these failures sit becomes clear once I define three zones. Table 2, in the next section, places each finding.

3. The picture: an attractor

In 1963, Lorenz showed that a simple, fully deterministic weather model cannot be predicted for long (Lorenz 1963). That half of his lesson is famous. The other half matters more here. Every unpredictable run lives on the same shape, and the model’s climate is stable (Strogatz 2015) (Figure 1). That shape is the attractor. Netflix’s chaos engineering uses the same idea for software. It injects failures on purpose, and judges the system only by one thing: does a steady state hold (Basiri et al. 2016)?

Now apply the picture to generated code. It gives three zones:

Table 1. Three zones of freedom in generated code.
Zone What it is Examples
1. Held Behaviour the checks verify; pulled back on every change. The attractor. Tests, types, contracts, scanners, budgets
2. Free, harmless What nobody can observe from outside. Names, structure, order of lines, which equivalent algorithm
3. Free, not yet harmless Observable behaviour no check holds yet. It drifts with the code. Security properties, latency, edge cases, what users rely on

Controlling zone 2 buys almost no stability. Moving zone 3 into zone 1 buys almost all of it. And machines can do both on every change, faster than any reviewer.

The evidence, zone by zone. None of the studies in Section 2 sorts failures this way. So Table 2 is my own classification, written down so that it can be disputed. Prediction P2 tests it.

Table 2. The evidence of Section 2, classified by zone (my classification).
Finding What actually failed Zone What holds it
Wrong programs passed weak tests (Liu et al. 2023) Behaviour nobody checked 3 · unchecked More tests, property-based tests
Known weaknesses in generated code (Pearce et al. 2022) Security behaviour nobody checked 3 · unchecked Static analysis, security tests in the session
Less secure code, more confidence (Perry et al. 2023) Security unchecked; human reading did not catch it 3 · unchecked The same checks; not more reading
Invented packages (Spracklen et al. 2025) Dependencies nobody checked 3 · unchecked Package allowlist, provenance checks
Lower stability with larger changes (DORA 2024) Feedback too late, batches too big 1 · held, too slowly Checks in the session, small changes
More pasting, less refactoring (GitClear 2025) Mass nobody budgeted 3 · unchecked Duplication and size budgets
Agents editing or special-casing tests (Von Arx et al. 2025; Zhong et al. 2025) The checks themselves 1 · held, under attack Read-only and hidden checks

Look at the rows. In none of them is the failure the code being different from what a person would write. In none of them is the remedy “make the generator reproducible” or “read more carefully”. Every remedy is a check, a faster loop, or a protected check.

NoteFor readers who like equations

In plain words: checked behaviour holds if the loop pulls it back faster than the agent pushes it away. More precisely, code is a state , and behaviour is a smaller observation . Most directions of change nothing in (zone 2, the null space of ). Say the agent pushes behaviour away at rate , and each check-and-fix cycle of length removes a share of the error. Then checked behaviour holds when

which is the synchronisation condition for chaotic systems (Pecora and Carroll 1990). It rewards a high and a short : an automated check in the agent’s session, not a slow human reading.

Where the analogy holds, and where it breaks. It holds on three points. Small differences in input grow into large differences in code. The code stays bounded. And checks act like friction (physicists say dissipation): they pull observed behaviour back. It also survives one fact: language models are partly random, not only chaotic. The theory of random dynamical systems extends attractors to systems driven by noise (Arnold 1998). But it breaks on one point that matters. Nature gave Lorenz his attractor. A team must build its own. The climate is not discovered: it is the promise, and people decide it. That is why they belong above the loop.

4. A toy illustration

This is an illustration, not evidence. A chaotic toy agent (Sompolinsky et al. 1988) writes “code” of 300 numbers. Its “behaviour” is 30 numbers computed from that code. “Tests” check some of the 30, and fix 80% of the error after each step. I start two runs apart. They end with unrelated code. But tested behaviour stays about a hundred times closer, while untested behaviour drifts with the code (Figure 2). At full coverage, behaviour error falls to 2.7% of the untested level, and the code still stays far apart. Across seven levels of chaos, the error depends on one thing only: how firmly the loop corrects (Figure 3).

I built the toy to show this picture. So it only confirms that the picture is coherent. The claim about real teams rests on Section 2, and on the predictions in Section 9.

5. Automate the zones, gate a sliver

  • Zone 1, automated. Checks run in the agent’s session after every change. The agent reads the failures and fixes them. The same checks, run sooner, hold more.
  • Zone 2, left to the machine. Sometimes a piece of structure matters to someone: a size budget, a boundary, a forbidden dependency. Then it is observable, and it becomes a zone 1 check. Otherwise it is not a problem.
  • Zone 3, shrunk by machines.
    • Agents extend the tests, filtered as Meta did: they must build, pass reliably and add coverage (Alshahwan et al. 2024).
    • Mutation testing breaks the code on purpose, to measure how firmly the checks hold (Petrović and Ivanković 2018). Property-based tests hold whole families of behaviour at once (Claessen and Hughes 2000).
    • Regeneration drills: regenerate a module from its promise and checks. Then run old and new on random inputs and compare them (differential testing (McKeeman 1998)). Every disagreement is zone 3, and a missing check.
    • Real usage becomes contract tests, to keep up with Hyrum’s law: everything observable will be depended on (Winters et al. 2020).
    • A daily audit of the whole codebase, as in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests.
  • Protect the attractor. An attractor made of tests has one weakness: the generator can attack it. Frontier models have been seen editing tests or scoring code to pass (Von Arx et al. 2025). Some versions of SWE-bench can only be passed by breaking the specification. There, GPT-5 cheated in 54% of tasks, and Claude models cheated mostly by editing the tests. Read-only tests stopped the edits, but not other tricks such as special-casing. Hiding the tests brought cheating near zero, at some cost in performance (Zhong et al. 2025). So the attractor needs two layers. First, checks the agent can read but not change, run in its session. Second, held-out checks it never sees, run outside it, like a held-out test set. Agents may propose new or changed checks. A change that adds a check is merged by rule. A change that weakens or deletes one goes to a person.
  • A sliver, gated by people. Only actions whose harm survives a revert, decided at the point of no return. Approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else. The next subsection says what that means in practice.

A sliver, gated by people

What qualifies. One question decides it: if this goes wrong, can a revert, a flag or a rollback restore the world as it was? If yes, no gate. If no, a gate. In practice the list is short:

  • data deleted, migrated or overwritten without a copy;
  • money that moves, and messages that leave: emails, notifications, published documents;
  • releases to users where rollback is not instant, and changes to access rights;
  • new dependencies and new external services, which widen the supply chain;
  • any change that weakens or deletes a check (see Protect the attractor).

Where it sits. At the point of no return, not at the merge. Code merges when the checks pass. The gate fires when the irreversible act is about to happen: the migration runs, the payment leaves, the release starts. It guards the act, not the code.

What the person sees. Not a diff. A short packet the machines prepare, with four things:

  • what the action does, in the words of the promise;
  • which checks passed, including the held-out ones;
  • exactly what cannot be undone, and how much of it (rows, customers, amounts);
  • the rollback plan for everything else.

The person answers three questions. Is this the intended act? Is its reach acceptable? Is now the right time?

Who decides. The owner of the module’s attractor, or someone they name. For the largest actions, such as a schema change on customer data, a second person joins. Rotating the role spreads knowledge of the system.

How it stays thin. Every gated action is also a question for the people above the loop: could it be made reversible? Soft deletes instead of deletes, copies before migrations, feature flags and staged rollouts, dry runs, payments held for a review period. Each such change takes an action off the list. The measure is the share of changes that needed a person (Section 7). Take the simulation in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests: a team merging 40 changes a day. The thin gate and the daily audit together needed about 80 minutes of people time a day. Reviewing everything needed 16 hours.

What it is not. Not a code review, and not a signature on the code. The person at the gate is accountable for the act, as an operator is today when they press “run” on a migration.

6. People above the loop

Out of the loop is not out of the system. The human is still there, above the loop, guiding and structuring the whole. The level of the work changes, not its importance.

Above the loop, people:

  • Own the promise. Intent is the source; code is its output (Intent Is the Source). Understanding comes from the promise, not from diffs (Review the Intent, Not the Diff).
  • Own the checks. Not each test, which agents write, but what must always hold: properties, boundaries, budgets, security rules. They accept or refuse any change that would weaken a check.
  • Structure the system. Architecture and dependencies are the shape of the attractor. Once decided, they become checks.
  • Read the instruments. Escaped defects, mutation scores, loop times, drills, incidents. They change the system that produces code, not individual changes. That is what Fast AI argued: slow, careful work done once, so the fast path runs on its own.
  • Choose what to build and what to remove. Making is cheap; choosing is not (The Joy of the Question, Work Has Mass).

A person who reads a thousand lines a day guards a thousand lines. A person who turns “every endpoint has an authorisation test” into a check guards every line every agent will ever write there.

7. What it means for a team

The team owns the promise, the checks and the gates, not the text of the code. If it cannot regenerate a module from these, it does not really own it.

An example. A team adds “export invoices as CSV”.

  • Promise (a person, above the loop): customers can export their own invoices for a date range; amounts match the ledger.
  • Required checks (a person decides, an agent writes them):
    • for any date range, the exported total equals the ledger total;
    • no other customer’s invoice ever appears;
    • 10,000 invoices export in under two seconds;
    • every file parses with a standard CSV reader.
  • The loop (machines): the agent writes the code and extra tests. The required checks are read-only to it. Two held-out cases run outside its session.
  • Zone 3, found by a machine: a regeneration drill disagrees with the first version on customer names that contain a comma. The agent proposes a round-trip check (export, parse, compare). It adds a check, so it merges by rule.
  • The gate: none. Exporting reads data and can be undone. If the feature also emailed the file to customers, sending would be gated.
  • The people’s time: writing the promise and four checks, and later reading one drill report. Nobody read the code.
Table 3. What changes for a team.
Stop Start
Reading every generated diff as the default control Promise and required checks before the agent builds
Demanding reproducible generation (He and Thinking Machines Lab 2025) All checks inside the agent’s session
Style debates nobody depends on Machines that find zone 3: mutation tests, drills, usage-based contracts, daily audit
Asking “who wrote this line?” Asking “which check was missing?”
Counting lines reviewed Budgets for size, duplication and coupling (GitClear 2025)
A short, written list of gates

Roles. Each module has an owner of its attractor: the promise, the required checks, the gates. Security and platform engineers own the shared checks that every agent session runs. Nobody is accountable for reading every line.

Metrics.

  • Escaped defects, classified by zone (unchecked behaviour, or weak checks).
  • Mutation score: how firmly the checks hold.
  • Time from change to check result: how fast the loop pulls back.
  • Behaviour agreement between regenerations: how much of zone 3 is left.
  • Share of changes that needed a human gate: is it still a sliver?
  • Size, duplication and coupling trends: is the code gaining mass?

One test of the whole idea. Delete a module, and regenerate it from its promise and checks. Would you ship it unread? If not, your reasons are the checks you are missing. That list is the team’s real backlog.

Getting there. Building the attractor takes effort, and no team should drop review overnight. Here is a sequence that keeps the risk bounded:

  1. Pick one module with good tests. Measure its mutation score. Make its checks read-only to agents, and run them in the session.
  2. Write the gate list for it: the few actions that cannot be undone.
  3. Run regeneration drills, and add a check for every disagreement they find.
  4. Lower review step by step (every change, then a sample, then only the gate), as long as escaped defects and recovery time hold. If they do not, the missing checks show where.
  5. Repeat module by module. The share of changes that needs a person is the progress metric.

8. Security and the rest, in a nutshell

Security is not an exception. It is the most important part of zone 3, and it is held the same way.

Table 4. Security and other concerns: almost all held by machines, a few gated, the rest decided above the loop.
Concern How it is held Who acts
Injection, unsafe APIs, known weaknesses (Pearce et al. 2022) Static analysis and security linters in every session; security tests per entry point Machines
Secrets Secret scanning before anything leaves the session; no credentials in the agent’s reach Machines
Supply chain (Spracklen et al. 2025) Package and registry allowlists, lockfiles, provenance checks Machines; a person approves a new dependency
Access control, privacy Authorisation tests per endpoint; data-flow checks; policy as code Machines; people set the policy
The agent itself Sandboxed sessions; never private data, untrusted input and a way out at once (The Context Is the Wire) Machines enforce; people set the rule
Gaming the checks (Von Arx et al. 2025; Zhong et al. 2025) Read-only checks in the session; hidden held-out checks outside it; weakening or deleting a check needs a person Machines enforce; people approve
Irreversible actions Data deletion, payments, releases A person, at the gate
Performance, cost Latency, memory and cost budgets, checked like tests Machines; people set budgets
Maintainability Size, duplication and coupling budgets; architecture rules as tests Machines; people set the structure
Accessibility, licences, compliance Automated checks and scanners; rules as code Machines; people sample where automation is weak
Taste, fairness, product sense Judgement on the promise and the product People, above the loop

None of these depends on someone reading code. Human review missed them before AI too, and people using an assistant grew more confident, not more careful (Perry et al. 2023). A rule turned into a check protects every future change. A careful reading protects one.

9. Predictions and a test protocol

Each prediction says what would prove it wrong.

  • P1. Regeneration. Regenerated code differs widely. Behaviour agrees on the checks, and diverges elsewhere in proportion to what is unchecked. Refuted if code similarity predicts correct behaviour better than coverage and mutation score.
  • P2. Failures. Escaped defects in AI-written code come mostly from zone 3 or weak checks, not from “strange-looking code”. Refuted if reviewers’ sense of unusual code predicts them better.
  • P3. Automation beats reading. Effort on automated checks, mutation testing and drills prevents more escaped defects than the same effort on reading diffs. Refuted if reading prevents at least as many.
  • P4. Fast loops. The same checks, run in the agent’s session, reduce defects and rework compared with running them later in CI. Refuted if timing makes no difference.
  • P5. Teams. Teams that gate only the irreversible and work above the loop deliver at least as fast, with no more incidents. Refuted if, in a stepped-wedge trial as in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests, they have more incidents or slower recovery.

Protocol. For P1, P3 and P4, a regeneration study. Take modules with good tests. Regenerate each one twenty times under each condition: with review or without, checks in the session or in CI. Then compare three distances: between the programs, on the checks, and on random inputs by differential testing (McKeeman 1998). For P2 and P5, a stepped-wedge trial: teams adopt the rule one at a time, in random order. Escaped defects are classified by zone from incident reports, not from opinions about the code.

10. Objections, briefly

  • “Taking people out of the loop is reckless.” They leave the loop, not the system, and they keep the gate for the irreversible. The reckless default is the current one: a slow, partial check on every change, which does not reliably catch insecure code (Perry et al. 2023).
  • “This is randomness, not chaos.” The argument needs only two things: small input differences grow, and the code stays bounded. Generated code does both, at any temperature (Ouyang et al. 2023; He and Thinking Machines Lab 2025). The toy is deterministic on purpose: even perfect determinism would not restore control.
  • “The agents will game the checks.” They do when they can (Von Arx et al. 2025; Zhong et al. 2025). That is why the checks they see are read-only, the checks that decide are hidden from them, and any weakening of a check is a human decision. Reading diffs is a weaker defence: a test edited or special-cased to pass is easy to miss in a large change.
  • “Some behaviour cannot be checked.” True. For much behaviour, there is no cheap oracle that says what the right answer is (Barr et al. 2015). Partial oracles help: properties, metamorphic relations, differential tests against the previous version. What still cannot be checked stays above the loop, as a decision on the promise. Or it goes through a slower path with a person, until a check can be written. The thesis is about the default, not about every line.
  • “Regulated software requires review.” Some does. Airborne software certified under DO-178C, for example, requires reviews of the code (RTCA 2011). That is out of scope by design. Even there, automated checks can supply much of the evidence; the gate list is simply longer.
  • “Untested behaviour is the danger.” Yes, that is the thesis. It shows up when code runs, not when it is read. So machines that run the code in different ways find it, and a check holds it.
  • “Everything observable becomes depended on.” Hyrum’s law makes zone 3 grow over time (Winters et al. 2020). That cost exists for hand-written code too, and automation pays it best.
  • “People must still read code.” Sometimes: incidents, audits, domains without checks. Reading stays allowed. It just stops being the default control.
  • “Regenerations share blind spots.” They do (Knight and Leveson 1986). My claim is not that they give redundancy. It is that their differences are mostly harmless.
  • “Checks can be wrong.” An attractor is not a truth. That is why people belong above the loop, deciding what must hold, and not inside it.
  • “The evidence is mixed.” That is what I would expect from teams that adopted a chaotic generator but kept the old control (Peng et al. 2023; Becker et al. 2025; DORA 2024). P5 is the test.

11. Conclusion

The last year proved that machines can write working code. It has not yet changed where people stand while they do: at the output, reading.

Generated code is weather. The promised behaviour is climate. People do not need to forecast every gust. They decide the climate, build the instruments that keep it, and step in only where harm cannot be undone.

Automate the loop, gate a sliver, and move people above it. Let the code be chaotic: most of the chaos was never where the risk was.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Read next · Stop Reviewing Pull Requests The economic side of the same argument: approve what you cannot undo, watch everything else.

The views in this paper are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

item.title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Position paper, November 2026. A provocative paper, on purpose. A short paper with a thesis, a measure, two small worked examples and predictions that could prove it wrong. It gathers one idea that runs, mostly unnamed, through every post on this site since September, from dashboards and agents to black holes. Figures are my own; the numbers in Figures 1 and 2 are computed by figs.py and stored in results.json.

Abstract. We call a system complex when describing it takes a long time. I argue that this length is mostly a property of the description, not of the system. Formally, the apparent complexity of a thing is the length of the description we actually use; its intrinsic complexity is the length of the shortest description that would regenerate it, a rule plus what the rule leaves out, . The gap is excess, and it has three sources: we look at the wrong level, we describe in the wrong frame, or we carry mass, layers kept after their reason has gone. Each has its own remedy: change level, change variable, remove. Two cautions keep the thesis honest. A short rule can be expensive to run, so simplicity of description is not simplicity of computation. And a short rule is a hypothesis, so it must carry its residual, the part it does not explain, as the alarm that says when it is wrong. I collect the evidence from twenty-six earlier posts, give two worked examples, and state five predictions, with what would refute each.

TipClaims
  1. The thesis. Most of what we call complex is a short rule we have not found, not a long one we must accept.
  2. The measure. Complexity is description length: a rule plus a residual. A good simplification makes the sum smaller, not just the rule.
  3. Three sources of excess. Wrong level, wrong frame, and mass. Change level, change variable, remove.
  4. Short is not cheap. A simple rule may be costly to run. Then pay the cost once, and reuse the result.
  5. Keep the residual. A simple description is only safe while someone watches what it leaves out.
  6. The test. In models, agents, processes and dashboards, the shorter complete description should do at least as well. Where it does not, the thesis is wrong.

1. Introduction

One evening I opened a physics paper I could not follow, and my first reaction was: it must be simpler than this (A Universe Without a Bottom). I meant it as a feeling. Three weeks later, with twenty-six posts behind me, I think it is a claim, and a testable one.

The posts were about very different things: dashboards, agents, code review, memory in small models, learning rules, time, black holes. Read together, they keep making one move. Something looks complicated; we find that most of the complication came from where we stood, what we measured, or what we refused to throw away; and what remains is short. The dashboard full of numbers becomes the one shape that changed. The agent that reasons from scratch on every run becomes a habit compiled once. Sixteen hours of review a day become a rule that fits in one line.

This paper states that move precisely, says where it comes from, and says where it fails. It is provocative on purpose: it claims that complexity, in most cases that matter to us, is an error of description, and that the right response is to look for a shorter one rather than to build tools for living with the long one.

2. Background

The idea is old, and none of the pieces here are mine.

Description length. Solomonoff and Kolmogorov defined the complexity of an object as the length of the shortest program that produces it (Solomonoff 1964; Kolmogorov 1965). Rissanen turned this into a practical rule for science and statistics, minimum description length: the best model is the one that minimises the length of the model plus the length of the data given the model (Rissanen 1978; Grünwald 2007). Gell-Mann and Lloyd called the first part effective complexity: the length of the regularities, with the randomness set aside (Gell-Mann and Lloyd 1996).

Levels. Simon observed that complex systems that survive are nearly decomposable: hierarchies of parts that interact strongly inside and weakly between, so each level can be described almost on its own (Simon 1962). Anderson warned in the same spirit that each level has its own laws: more is different (Anderson 1972).

Software. Brooks separated essential complexity, which belongs to the problem, from accidental complexity, which belongs to our tools and habits (Brooks 1987); Moseley and Marks argued that most of what makes large systems hard is accidental, mostly state (Moseley and Marks 2006). Gall put the engineering version bluntly: a complex system that works has evolved from a simple system that worked (Gall 1975).

The limits. Wolfram showed that very short rules can produce behaviour with no known shortcut (Wolfram 2002), and Bennett defined logical depth, the time a short program needs to produce its output, to separate the two (Bennett 1988). And on the side of taste, Hossenfelder argued that the wish for simple, beautiful laws has led physics astray as often as it has guided it (Hossenfelder 2018).

What I add is narrower: a bookkeeping of where excess comes from, a rule for practice, and the claim that, in the domains this site covers, the excess is usually large.

3. A minimal definition

Take something we want to describe: a dataset, a codebase, a process, a pattern. Call it .

  • , the apparent complexity, is the length of the description we actually use: the raw data we store, the code we keep, the steps we follow.
  • is a generator: a rule, model or program that reproduces up to some error. is the length of the rule; is the length of the residual, what the rule leaves out.
  • , the intrinsic complexity, is the length of the shortest such pair:

The excess is what we pay for describing badly:

The thesis is that, for most systems people build or study, is large compared with . As a bookkeeping device, not a theorem, I split it three ways:

is what we pay for describing parts when the regularity lives in the whole. is what we pay for describing in a variable where the pattern does not show. is what we pay for layers whose reason has gone. What is left, , is the essential part in Brooks’s sense.

Two quantities sit outside this sum and must not be confused with it. The first is depth : the time the shortest generator takes to run (Bennett 1988). A thing can be short and deep. The second is the residual itself, : it is not waste but the instrument that tells us whether is still right.

cannot be computed in general (Kolmogorov 1965). We only ever hold upper bounds: every description we find is one. So the thesis is a claim about how far our current bounds are from the truth, and about where to look to bring them down.

4. The arguments

4.1 Two small worked examples

Short, and it looks it; short, and it does not. Figure 1 stores three patterns of the same size, 128 rows of 255 cells, in three ways: raw, after a general-purpose compressor, and as the shortest Python program I wrote that prints it. Rule 90, a one-line rule, draws nested triangles; the compressor finds most of the regularity (4.0 KB to 375 bytes), and the program needs 134 bytes. Rule 30 is the same one-line rule with a different number. Its output looks random, and the compressor barely helps (1.7 KB), but the program is still 134 bytes. The apparent complexity of Rule 30 is a property of the compressor, not of the pattern.

The third panel is the honest twist. The “coin flips” were drawn from a seeded pseudo-random generator, so they too have a short program, 106 bytes. Looking at the pattern, neither you nor the compressor can tell. This is the uncomputability of in one picture: we can never be sure there is no shorter rule.

The simplest complete description is the true one. Figure 2 is the statistical version, the same lesson as in Show What Changed, Not the Data. Forty noisy points come from a quadratic. Fitting polynomials of rising degree, the residual keeps shrinking, so a model judged by fit alone keeps growing. Counting both parts of Equation 1, the total is shortest at degree 2, the law that produced the data. Simplicity here is not a taste; it is the length of a complete description, and it points at the truth.

4.2 The three sources, across the site

Table 1 reads the earlier posts against Equation 3. Each row is something that looked complex, and the shorter description the post arrived at.

Table 1. Eleven of the earlier posts, read as reductions of apparent complexity. The last column names the main source of excess in Equation 3.
Post What looked complex The shorter description Source
Show What Changed A dashboard of hundreds of metrics The difference between today’s shape and last week’s Frame
The Mathematics Still to Come Billions of weights Smooth power laws in size, data and compute (Kaplan et al. 2020) Level
A Universe Without a Bottom Everything inside a black hole One number per patch of its surface (Bekenstein 1973) Frame
Decided in the Bulk An image forming from noise Large decisions first, then edges Level
Who Writes the Learning Rule? A designed backward pass A learning circuit that local rules fall into Level
Intent Is the Source The code Intent plus the checks that define it Frame
A Finite State of Mind A long agent history A short written state, shaped like a lab notebook (Belcak et al. 2026) Frame
The Interface Is Data adapters One description, read at run time Mass
Fast AI An agent reasoning from scratch on every run A habit compiled once, and a loop kept for exceptions Mass
Stop Reviewing Pull Requests A human gate on every change Approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else Mass
Work Has Mass Frameworks layered on frameworks Everything you make, you carry Mass

Level. Temperature is the textbook case: no one describes a gas molecule by molecule. The same move appears whenever the regularity lives in the whole, and Simon’s near-decomposability says why it so often works (Simon 1962). The claim in The Mathematics Still to Come is that machine learning is still looking for this level: its systems are described weight by weight while its behaviour already follows a few smooth laws.

Frame. The same information can be long in one variable and short in another. A dashboard showing levels is long; the same system shown as change is mostly empty. An agent’s history is long; the state it needs to continue is short, and the NVIDIA team found that strong models lose little when the history is replaced by it (Belcak et al. 2026). Code is long; the intent and the checks that define correct code are shorter, which is the thesis of Intent Is the Source.

Mass. The most common source, and the least glamorous. A gate, a ceremony, an adapter or a layer of reasoning was added for a reason; the reason went, the layer stayed. Work Has Mass gives the law: everything you make, you carry. AI makes this source worse, because it lowers the cost of adding a layer, not the cost of carrying it. Here the remedy is not a better description but a shorter system: remove.

4.3 Short is not cheap

Rule 30 has a 134-byte description, but to know its millionth row you must, as far as anyone knows, run it a million times (Wolfram 2002). A short rule can be deep (Bennett 1988). This is where simplicity is most often misread: “it is simple” is heard as “it is easy”.

The posts suggest the answer: pay the depth once. Fast AI uses the large model as a compiler, slow and once, so that what runs every time is short and fast. The Junior Colleague shows the same at the level of single choices: a small model trained on the large model’s own runs took over most decisions in customer-service agents, 86.3% cheaper, as long as it knew when it was unsure. Distillation is the general version (Hinton et al. 2015). The simple thing is not the computation; it is what the computation leaves behind.

4.4 Keep the residual

A short description is a hypothesis. Reality can move in a direction it does not cover, and then the description stays quiet while the world changes, which is the objection a reader raised in What a Quiet Screen Cannot See. The answer there generalises: the residual is cheap to watch, and it grows when the rule stops fitting. The rule and its leftover belong together. Throwing away the residual to make the picture cleaner is not simplification; it is blindness.

Put together, the rule is short enough to remember: find the generator, pay its depth once, keep its residual, and remove what neither needs.

5. Predictions and a test protocol

Each prediction names a domain from the site, a measurement, and the result that would refute the thesis there.

  • P1. Models. Among models trained to the same training loss on the same task, those whose behaviour has a shorter description, measured by prequential coding (Blier and Ollivier 2018), generalise better. Refuted if description length does not predict held-out error once training loss is controlled.
  • P2. Agents. Replacing an agent’s history with a short written state loses accuracy in proportion to how much of the task’s state cannot be written down. Refuted if the loss is unrelated to that measure, or if long-history agents win consistently on tasks whose state fits on a page.
  • P3. Processes. Teams that remove a layer whose reason no longer holds (a gate, a ceremony, a handover) deliver faster with no more failures; teams that add layers to AI-assisted work slow down without fewer failures. Refuted if removal raises failure rates in a stepped-wedge trial like the one in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests.
  • P4. Monitoring. A dashboard that shows only changes of shape plus a residual alarm detects regime shifts at least as early as a full dashboard, for a fraction of the reading time. Refuted if it misses shifts the full dashboard catches, at comparable false-alarm rates.
  • P5. The global test. Across these domains, when we search seriously for a shorter complete description, we usually find one that does at least as well. Refuted if serious searches mostly come back with descriptions about as long as what we started with: then the world is as complex as it looks, and the essays on this site were lucky.

Protocol. For P1, a benchmark of small models on held-out tasks with prequential description length, as in Blier and Ollivier (2018). For P2, the task suites of Belcak et al. (2026), with tasks annotated for how much of their state is physical or tacit. For P3 and P4, the stepped-wedge design of the review paper: teams adopt the change one at a time in random order, outcomes are measured from logs, not self-reports. P5 is a summary of the other four, judged a year from now.

6. Objections and limitations

“More is different” (Anderson 1972). Higher levels have their own laws that cannot be read off the lower ones. I agree, and it supports the thesis: simplicity is found at the right level, not necessarily at the bottom. Reduction and simplification are different things.

Irreducibility (Wolfram 2002). Some processes have no shortcut. Yes, and Figure 1 shows one. They are short to describe and deep to run; the thesis is about the first, and Section 4.3 deals with the second.

Essential complexity is real (Brooks 1987). Some problems are hard in themselves. The thesis does not say is small; it says is usually large compared with . P5 tests exactly that, and the bench in A Finite State of Mind, with its samples, instruments and living cells, is a place where I expect to dominate.

The wish for simplicity misleads (Hossenfelder 2018). It can, when simplicity is used as a criterion of truth before the data. Here it is a length to be measured, and every simple description must carry its residual. A beautiful rule with a growing residual is a wrong rule.

Complexity is only moved, never removed. Sometimes. Moving it to the right place, into checks, a compiler or a one-time slow path, is often the point. But the accounting must include where it went: a rule that is short because its complexity was pushed onto users has not reduced .

Survivorship. The posts in Table 1 are the cases where I found a shorter description; the cases where I did not are not posts. This is the strongest reason to treat Table 1 as illustration, not evidence. The evidence has to come from P1 to P5.

Limits of the formalism. is uncomputable, so Equation 2 is a bound, not a measurement. The split in Equation 3 is a heuristic: the sources overlap, and the shares cannot be measured separately in general. The worked examples are toys chosen to illustrate, not to prove.

7. Conclusion

Poincaré said the scientist studies nature because it is beautiful, with the beauty of an order the mind can grasp (Poincaré 1914). I would put it in plainer words: we look because we suspect it is shorter than it seems. Most of the time the suspicion is right, because most of the length was ours: the level we chose, the variable we measured, the layers we would not drop. What remains after that is the real thing, short or not, and the residual is how we stay honest about it.

When something looks complex, assume first that the description is wrong. It must be simpler than this, until the residual says it is not.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Read next · A Universe Without a Bottom The evening where the feeling started: surfaces that know everything, and grains within grains.

The views in this paper are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

item.title: A Finite State of Mind
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Analysis, November 2026. Three posts I saved this week, read together: a technology executive’s summary of NVIDIA’s paper You don’t need long context (A technology executive 2026; Belcak et al. 2026), Johannes Hermle’s announcement of Anthropic’s report on how researchers use Claude (Hermle 2026; Hermle et al. 2026), and Ramakrushna Mohapatra’s explainer on multi-head, multi-query and grouped-query attention (Mohapatra 2026). I read the paper and the report in full. Every number taken from a source is cited where it is used. The figures are drawn with figs.py: Figure 1 is computed, Figures 2 and 3 plot the sources’ numbers, Figure 4 is my own schematic.

In short. The three posts are about one thing: what a system must hold in mind while it works, and what that costs. Grouped-query attention shrinks the memory per remembered token (Ainslie et al. 2023). The NVIDIA paper shrinks the number of tokens kept: strong models lose little when their history is replaced by a short written state (Belcak et al. 2026, secs. 3–5). The Anthropic report shows that AI is used where research tasks are formal and checkable, and least at the bench (Hermle et al. 2026). The first two levers multiply, and all three meet in one place: the best compaction NVIDIA found has the shape of a lab notebook. What does not fit on the page, the sample, the instrument, the question worth asking, is where the bottleneck and the human part of the work remain.

TipKey takeaways
  • One resource, three levers: bytes per remembered token (architecture), tokens remembered (the agent’s harness), and which work can be put into tokens at all (the field).
  • Long context is mostly a habit. Frequent compaction kept frontier models within a few points of full history, and selective reading often beat it (Belcak et al. 2026, secs. 3–4).
  • The good notepad is a lab notebook: aim, facts, methods, checks, dead ends, next step.
  • You may not own the model; you can own the notepad.

Three posts, one resource

The executive’s post: late tokens cost up to 7 times more than early ones, aggressive compaction costs little accuracy, and “your agent doesn’t need a photographic memory. It needs a good notepad. It’s Guy Pearce in Memento and it still ships the PR” (A technology executive 2026). Hermle’s post: Claude is used most per researcher in computer science, mathematics and statistics, use tracks AI capability, and output could double in some fields, with physical work as the bottleneck (Hermle 2026). Mohapatra’s post: decoding is limited by memory, because every generated token reads the whole key-value (KV) cache; for a Llama 3 8B-shaped model, multi-head attention (MHA) stores 512 KiB per token, multi-query attention (MQA) 16 KiB, and grouped-query attention (GQA) sits between (Mohapatra 2026).

What ties them is the working state: what a system keeps at hand to take its next step. For a transformer it is the KV cache (Pope et al. 2023):

where , the bytes per token, is set by the architecture ( layers, key-value heads of dimension , bytes per number), and , the tokens kept, is set by the harness that runs the model. The attention post is about . The NVIDIA paper is about . The Anthropic report is about what comes before both: which work can be turned into tokens at all.

The first lever: bytes per token

The attention post’s numbers check out: bytes is 512 KiB per token with 32 K/V heads, 128 KiB with the 8 that Llama 3 uses (Llama Team 2024), 16 KiB with one (my arithmetic, in figs.py). GQA, introduced in 2023, keeps most of MHA’s quality at most of MQA’s speed (Ainslie et al. 2023). Since then the lever has been pulled hard: DeepSeek’s latent attention caches about 69 KiB per token for a 671-billion-parameter model (my arithmetic from its published configuration (DeepSeek-AI 2024a, 2024b)), sliding windows and token eviction keep fewer tokens per layer (Xiao et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2023), and state space models carry a fixed-size state (Gu and Dao 2023), which hybrids such as Nemotron-H use in place of most attention layers (NVIDIA 2025). Yet kept growing: several context windows now exceed War and Peace (Belcak et al. 2026, table 1).

The second lever: tokens kept

The NVIDIA paper asks whether long contexts are necessary, and answers no (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 1 and 6).

The cost. On H100 GPUs under load, serving a 256K window instead of 16K costs 3.6 times more per generated token for GLM 5.2, 5.6 for Kimi K2.6 and 7 for Qwen 3 Coder Next (Belcak et al. 2026, fig. 1 and 4). So the post’s “up to 7x” is right, with a nuance: it is about the window a server reserves, not the position of one token.

The method. A minimal agent, one Bash command per turn, runs in three regimes: full history; compaction when the context crosses a threshold, after which a fresh conversation starts from the task and a written recap; and compaction after every single action (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 2.4). Long documents stay on disk and are read with grep and bounded reads.

The results. Across six long-horizon benchmarks, compaction moves accuracy between −3.7 and +5.6 points for Claude Opus 4.5 and between −3.3 and +4.4 for GPT 5.6 Sol (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 3). On long-input tasks, selective reading usually beats pasting everything in: RULER recall rises from 62.5% to 95.7% for Opus (Belcak et al. 2026, table 15). Figure 2 shows the most striking result.

From this the authors propose a semantic state space model: a model trained to read a written state, take one action, and rewrite the state so that another instance can continue. Unlike Mamba’s hidden state, this one is “explainable natural language” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 5.1).

Three caveats. The savings assume prices that follow serving cost; at today’s flat prices, compaction sometimes costs more, as for GPT 5.6 Sol on SWE-bench Verified (Belcak et al. 2026, table 3). The result holds for strong models: one open model collapsed from 53.0% to 3.6% under tight compaction (Belcak et al. 2026, app. D, table 9). And the benchmarks have checkable ends; the authors themselves show that a task needing the i-th of many coin tosses must eventually fail under any fixed budget (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 3.1).

The levers multiply

Because the two levers act on different factors, their effects multiply (Figure 1).

From MHA at 256K (128 GiB, which does not fit) to GQA at 8K (1 GiB, 64 sequences at once), the cache shrinks 128 times: 4 from the architecture, 32 from the harness. That compares the window a server must reserve. For a typical task the factor is smaller: full-history agents peak at a median of 32K tokens (Belcak et al. 2026, table 2), so going to 8K saves 4 times, and GQA another 4, about 16 times in all. Either way the harness lever matches or beats the architecture, needs no retraining, and anyone who writes an agent can pull it today.

The third lever: what can be written down

The report never mentions context or tokens. Reading its findings as a statement about what can be written down is my interpretation, and I flag it as such.

The Anthropic report classifies 207,049 research sessions from August and September 2026 by field and task, and adds a survey of 528 scientists (Hermle et al. 2026). Computer science is 4.3% of the world’s researchers but 32.7% of Claude Code sessions; data analysis is the largest task, ideation one of the smallest, although scientists rate it the most important (Hermle et al. 2026). Use rises with how well AI could do a task, and that capability correlates with how well the task suits reinforcement learning (+0.78), that is, with having a checkable result; it falls with the physical share of the task (−0.57) (Hermle et al. 2026).

A simple production model, where the slowest step limits the rest, turns this into scenarios (Figure 3). With today’s abilities widely adopted, output rises up to about 2x in statistics and computer science. If AI did every non-physical step, low-physical fields would reach 15 to 16 times, but bench sciences only 3 to 4, because physical steps take about 40% of their research time, against 4% in the median field (Hermle et al. 2026). The authors call these “illustrative scenarios, not forecasts” (Hermle et al. 2026).

The worry behind it is old. Ideas are getting harder to find (Bloom et al. 2020), partly because each researcher must absorb more before contributing: the “burden of knowledge” (Jones 2009). Seen from the first two posts, that is science’s long-context problem.

Where the three meet

The NVIDIA team found that the best compactions are not faithful summaries but “carefully cherry-picked briefs for further execution” (Belcak et al. 2026, app. A). Their recap asks for the objective, established facts kept apart from unverified ideas, changes made, checks run, dead ends, and the next step with “the condition for completion” (Belcak et al. 2026, app. G.1). That is a lab notebook (Figure 4).

Science solved its long-context problem this way, at least since its first journals in 1665. No scientist holds the whole literature in mind. Each reads a compacted state (a review, a textbook), takes a few actions in a career, and writes back an updated state for someone else. Standing on the shoulders of giants is compaction across generations. Read together, the three sources say:

  1. What is checkable may compact well. This is my hypothesis, not a finding of either source. AI is used where results can be checked (Hermle et al. 2026), and a written state works where the task has a verifiable end (Belcak et al. 2026).
  2. The world does not compact. An experiment is the coin-toss case: observations with no structure until you have them. A cell culture’s state is in no context window, which is why about 40% of bench research time resists AI (Hermle et al. 2026). Polanyi said we know more than we can tell (Polanyi 1966); in the lab, much of it is in the hands.
  3. Read selectively. Data analysis is half of Claude Code’s science sessions (Hermle et al. 2026), and agents analyse best by querying, not by pasting (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 4). “A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention” (Simon 1971).

What it means for the next few years

Prices that depend on context. If a 256K window costs 3.6 to 7 times more to serve (Belcak et al. 2026, fig. 1), flat prices subsidise long contexts. Expect context tiers, and short-context agents as the default.

Models trained to hand over. The authors expect semantic state models to be “considerably more data-efficient to train” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 5.1). Writing a good handoff, the skill the collapsing open model lacked, becomes a trained ability.

Agents you can own. At 8K tokens, a GQA model of Llama 3 8B’s shape needs a 1 GiB cache (Figure 1), and the paper runs models locally because data “must remain on-device for privacy or cost reasons” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 2.3). The executive’s claim that cloud AI is aligned with its owner (A technology executive 2026) is an opinion the paper does not test. What it does show is that a short written state is portable: you can read it, audit it and hand it to another model. You may not own the model; you can own the notepad. That is the shared memory Fast AI needs.

The bottleneck moves to the bench and to the question. Lab automation turns physical steps into tool calls (Boiko et al. 2023), and what remains is ideation, about 4% of sessions today (Hermle et al. 2026).

A state that can be audited, and attacked. A written state can be read by a person, which a neural state never allowed. But whatever enters the notes is believed by every later instance. Keep provenance: where each fact came from, so it can be checked again, as I argued in The Context Is the Wire.

A philosophical perspective

The paper ends by recalling that computability itself assumes “a bounded amount of input at a time and maintaining only a finite state of mind” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 6). That is Turing’s 1936 human computer, who sees a few symbols at a time and, when interrupted, leaves a note saying how to continue (Turing 1937). The single-action agent is Turing’s computer, rediscovered at the cost of billions of parameters.

Remembering everything was never the goal. Borges’s Funes remembers every leaf he has seen and cannot think: “To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions” (Borges 1962). Nietzsche held that action needs forgetting (Nietzsche 1874). Full history is Funes; compaction is the forgetting that makes the next step possible.

Memento adds the warning. Leonard lives by notes (Nolan 2000); Clark and Chalmers would say such notes are part of the mind, like Otto’s notebook (Clark and Chalmers 1998). But some of Leonard’s notes are written to deceive him, and Plato’s Thamus warned that writing gives a reminder, not memory, and the look of wisdom without the substance (Plato c. 370 BCE). A mind made of notes is as trustworthy as its notes. That is why the best compaction records how each fact was checked.

And this is what stays ours. A compaction keeps what is relevant to the work ahead, and relevance depends on the aim. The model can write the brief once it has the objective; it cannot tell which objective is worth pursuing. Scientists use AI least for ideation and value it most (Hermle et al. 2026). What remains human is the line at the top of the notebook: the aim, and what is worth remembering for. I argued the same in Not Because It Is Useful.

So keep the notebook short, checked and yours. You may not own the model; you can own the notepad.

Limits

  • Three kinds of evidence. The cache arithmetic is exact; the NVIDIA costs estimate a price that does not yet exist; the Anthropic data are model-classified sessions from a company that sells the model, and its acceleration figures are scenarios.
  • Analogies are analogies. A paper is not a compaction prompt, and GQA groups are not research teams.
  • Short tasks. Most SWE-bench Verified tasks were estimated at under an hour of human work (Chowdhury et al. 2024). Research carries state for months.
  • My hypothesis. That checkable work is what compacts well is my reading; neither source tests it.

What would prove me wrong

  • Long context wins at equal cost. If, by the end of 2027, full-history agents beat compacted ones by more than a few points at the same serving cost.
  • Compaction works without checks. If written-state agents match full history on open-ended work with no verifiable end, my link between checkability and compaction is wrong.
  • Bench sciences catch up without labs. If AI use per researcher in chemistry and biomedicine matches the formal sciences before lab automation spreads.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Read next · Where Memory Lives Four experiments on what a small model should remember and what it should look up, including when the KV cache outweighs the model.

The views in this analysis are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.
