item.title: A Grammar for Tools
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, October 2026. A follow-up to The Interface Is Data. The figures are my own, drawn with figs.py; all are schematics except Figure 3, which is plain counting. The roles, relations and JSON in Figures 2, 6 and 7 are a proposal of mine, not part of the MCP specification.

In short. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gave AI agents a dictionary. Every tool defines itself: a name, a description, a schema for what it takes and what it returns. What MCP does not have is a grammar, a way to say how tools combine: which one must come first, which one feeds which, which ones are used together, which ones replace each other, and which ones must never meet in the same task. Today every agent rebuilds that grammar inside its context window, on every run, and forgets it at the end. With a few dozen tools that works. With thousands it does not, and the usual fix, searching tool descriptions, finds tools that look like the request, not tools that complete each other. I argue that the missing piece is a kind of object, the relation between tools, published as data. A useful grammar works at two levels: rules about kinds of tools (“anything that pays requires an approval”), which carry over to tools nobody has used yet, and habits of specific tools, learned from use. Relations can come from four sources (schemas, authors, use and policy), and each source has its own owner and its own level of trust. None of this is new in principle: OpenAPI has links between operations, its sister specification Arazzo (2024) writes down whole workflows, and the semantic web services of the 2000s described preconditions and effects. The older efforts stalled because writing a precise grammar cost too much and nothing could read an imprecise one. A language model can. The design principles come from neural networks (locality, sparse activation, plasticity, modularity and gating), but I no longer think we need to train a network to apply them.

TipKey takeaways
  • MCP is a dictionary. Each tool is defined on its own. The links between tools exist only inside one agent’s run.
  • The missing object is the relation. MCP has first-class tools, resources and prompts, and groups of tools are being proposed. It has no typed relation between tools, so nobody can publish, share, version or check one.
  • Resemblance is not complementarity. Searching descriptions finds tools like the request. A task needs tools that complete each other, and those rarely look alike. Tool-retrieval research since 2024 says the same.
  • The bottleneck is already visible. 2025 benchmarks with hundreds of MCP tools find that finding the right tool is the dominant failure, and that planning across steps and servers remains hard.
  • A grammar has two levels. Rules over roles (“pays requires approves”) hold for tools never seen before. Habits of named tools (“this payment tool is usually followed by that converter”) are sharp for known work and silent for new work.
  • Four sources, four owners. Edges are computed from schemas by any reader, declared by servers, observed by clients and imposed by the organisation’s gateway. Every edge should say where it came from.
  • This was tried before, in part. OpenAPI links, Arazzo workflows and semantic web services described how operations connect. Arazzo and agents.json write sentences (fixed workflows), not a grammar. The older efforts lacked a reader that could use a cheap, imperfect grammar. A language model is that reader.
  • Edges are local; names are not. Like links on the web, relations need no central map, but they do need stable names, which means a registry.
  • Borrow principles from neural networks, not the network. Locality, sparse activation, plasticity, modularity and gating describe how the grammar should behave. A learned router is an optimisation for later.

1. Points on a plane

Think of every MCP tool as a point. Its position is its meaning, what its description says it does. Two invoice tools sit close together; an invoice tool and a calendar tool sit far apart. A server publishes a handful of such points. A client connects to several servers and sees the union: a cloud of points with no lines between them (Model Context Protocol 2025c).

This is not a flaw. It is what made MCP so easy to adopt. A server does not need to know who else exists. Anyone can add a point, and every client can read it. That is the strength I described in The Interface Is Data: the interface became data, read when it is used.

But a task is never a point. “Pay this supplier invoice in euros and let them know” is a path: approve the invoice, convert the amount, pay, post the ledger entry, send a message. That path crosses three or four servers. Somebody has to draw it.

Today, the agent draws it. The model reads the tool descriptions, reasons about the task and chooses each call. The path exists, but only in one place and for one moment: the context window of one run. When the run ends, the path is gone. The next agent facing the same task draws it again from scratch.

2. A dictionary without a grammar

A better image than points is language. MCP gives us a dictionary. Each entry defines one word clearly and in a standard form. What a dictionary does not tell you is how to build a sentence: which words go together, in what order, which ones can stand in for each other, which combinations are wrong. That is the job of a grammar.

So what is missing from MCP is not an algorithm. It is a kind of object. MCP has first-class tools, resources and prompts. It has no first-class relation between them. As long as relations are not part of the vocabulary, nobody can publish one, share one, version one or check one. Every agent keeps its own private grammar, and nobody else can read it.

Resemblance is not complementarity

The current answer to large catalogues is search. Tools stay out of the context and are found by matching the request against their descriptions (Anthropic 2025c; Gan and Sun 2025), sometimes server first, then tool (Fei et al. 2025). This finds tools that resemble the request. A task needs tools that complete each other.

“Pay this supplier invoice in euros” resembles the invoice tools. It does not resemble the ledger or the mail server, yet the task needs both. The relation between paying an invoice and posting a ledger entry is not in either description. It is in the use.

Recommender systems learned this long ago. Shops distinguish products that substitute for each other (two similar cameras) from products that complement each other (a camera and a memory card), and the two kinds of relation have to be learned differently (McAuley et al. 2015). The oldest working answer, “customers who bought this also bought that”, does not look at descriptions at all: it counts what is used together (Linden et al. 2003). Tool retrieval has rediscovered the point. COLT showed in 2024 that matching a request to tool descriptions returns redundant tools and misses the complementary ones a multi-part request needs, and proposed retrieval aimed at the complete set (Qu et al. 2024). Tool2Vec embeds each tool from the requests that actually used it rather than from its description, and recalls far better (Moon et al. 2024). Both learn from use; both keep what they learn inside one system. Tool search in production is still mostly stuck at the first kind of relation. A grammar is how we write down the second, in a form others can read.

3. Why it matters now

With a few dozen tools, the agent can read every definition and draw the path itself. Nothing needs to be stored, nothing goes stale. The cost appears when catalogues grow, and two things grow with them.

The first is the cost of looking. MCP-Zero counts about 4,600 tokens for the 26 tools of the GitHub server alone (Fei et al. 2025). A thousand tools fill a large context window before the task has begun.

The second is the space of compositions. With tools there are ordered chains of of them. The chains anyone actually uses are a vanishing fraction of that space. The useful structure is small, roughly linear in , but nobody writes it down. So every run looks for it again inside a space that grows with the fourth power.

This is no longer a projection. LiveMCPBench gave agents 70 MCP servers and 527 tools across 95 everyday tasks. The best model completed 79% of them, most models only 30% to 50%, and the authors identify finding the right tool as the dominant bottleneck (Mo et al. 2025). MCP-Bench connected 20 models to 250 tools on 28 live servers, in tasks that chain tools within and across servers, and found persistent difficulty with long-horizon planning, with weaker models degrading most on multi-server tasks (Wang et al. 2025). Both point at the same gap: knowing which tools go together.

The field has noticed, and the answers so far tell the story:

  • Groups. A proposal for MCP, SEP-1300, lets servers put tools into groups and tags, so a client can load one functional area at a time (Model Context Protocol 2025e). Groups are sets: they say which tools belong together, not how they combine. They are the right first step, and relations are the natural next one.
  • Prompts. MCP servers can already publish prompts, templated workflows written in prose (Model Context Protocol 2025c). A prompt is a sentence, not a grammar: it lives on one server, is chosen by the user and cannot be checked or combined with prompts from other servers.
  • Skills. Agent Skills package instructions, scripts and tool use for one job (Anthropic 2025b). Each skill contains a small grammar, written by hand, for one bundle.
  • Research systems walk graphs of tool transitions learned from past runs (Liu et al. 2024), follow dependency edges after a first search (Lumer et al. 2025), or learn tool representations from use (Qu et al. 2024; Moon et al. 2024), each inside one system. Benchmarks such as TaskBench already describe tasks as tool graphs, with tools as nodes and dependencies as edges (Shen et al. 2024): the research community models the grammar, but only to evaluate agents, not to publish it.

Each of these holds a piece of the grammar. None can be read by anyone else, because the protocol has nowhere to put a relation. The protocol itself has moved fast: tool annotations arrived in March 2025 (Model Context Protocol 2025b), output schemas in June (Model Context Protocol 2025c), and the November 2025 revision added icons, guidance on tool names and long-running tasks (Model Context Protocol 2025d). None of them adds relations between tools. The 2026 roadmap focuses on transport, agent communication, governance and enterprise readiness (Model Context Protocol 2026); as far as I can tell, typed relations are not on it.

4. This was tried before

Describing how operations connect is an old idea, and it is worth asking why it did not take hold.

OpenAPI links. Since version 3.0, an OpenAPI description can say that a value returned by one operation is the input of another, with the exact field mapping: the id in the response of createUser becomes the userId parameter of getUser (OpenAPI Initiative 2017). That is precisely the feeds relation of this essay, standardised in 2017. It exists, it works, and few people use it. REST APIs got links between operations; MCP tools never did.

Arazzo and agents.json. In 2024 the OpenAPI Initiative published Arazzo, a specification for describing multi-step workflows across APIs: which operations to call, in which order, and how outputs become inputs (OpenAPI Initiative 2024). In 2025, agents.json built on OpenAPI to give AI agents “flows” and “links” for the same purpose (Wildcard AI 2025). These are the closest relatives of this essay, and they show that the need is real. But they write down sentences, complete workflows chosen in advance. They do not give a grammar from which an agent can build a sentence nobody wrote, and they say nothing about what was observed in use or forbidden by policy. A grammar and a set of sentences are complementary: a known workflow is a sentence the grammar allows, and a good workflow format is a natural way to publish one.

Semantic web services. In the early 2000s, OWL-S and WSMO described web services with inputs, outputs, preconditions and effects, so that software agents could find and compose them automatically (Martin et al. 2004; Bruijn et al. 2005). “Requires” is a precondition; “feeds” is an output matched to an input. The vision was close to this essay’s. It stalled, for two reasons: writing formal descriptions in shared ontologies cost far more than anyone would pay, and the reasoners that consumed them broke on anything imprecise.

What changed is the reader, the same argument I made in The Interface Is Data for self-describing APIs. A language model does not need a perfect ontology. It can use a relation that is partial, approximate or written in plain words, and weigh it against everything else it knows. And one of the four sources below, observed use, needs no author at all. A grammar that was too expensive to write precisely for a strict reader becomes cheap enough to write roughly for a tolerant one.

5. Where the grammar comes from

If relations are to become data, the first questions are where they come from and who keeps them. I see four sources. They differ in cost, in trust, and in who owns them.

5.1 Computed from types

Since its June 2025 revision, MCP lets a tool declare an outputSchema, the shape of what it returns, next to its inputSchema (Model Context Protocol 2025c). That is enough to derive some edges with no one declaring anything. If one tool returns a payment_id and another requires one, the first probably feeds the second.

Computed edges are cheap, and anyone can derive them: the client, a gateway, a catalogue. They are also checkable, since a test can confirm that the output of one tool still fits the input of the other. Their limits are real. They find data flow, not intent; field names are noisy; and output schemas are optional in MCP. I have not measured how many public servers declare them today. If few do, this source is a promise rather than a resource, and the first practical step is simply to publish output schemas.

5.2 Declared by authors

Some relations only the author knows. That paying requires an approval first. That schedule_payment is an alternative to paying now. That a tool is usually followed by a notification. These are short statements, and MCP already lets a tool carry extra metadata where they could live. They belong to the server, and travel with its tools.

Declared edges carry intent, which no other source has. They are also partial, since an author sees only their own side of a workflow, and they can be self-serving: every server has a reason to declare edges toward itself.

5.3 Observed in use

Every agent already draws the grammar on every run. If clients kept the paths they walked, they could count which tools are used together and turn the counts into weights. This is the truest source: it shows what actually happens, including partners nobody thought to declare.

It is also the most sensitive. What an organisation’s agents do is private, so observed edges belong to the client and stay inside the organisation by default, shared only as aggregated weights if at all. Counting them the same way everywhere needs a common trace format. That could be part of MCP, or a convention in an existing tracing standard such as OpenTelemetry; what matters is that it is shared.

5.4 Imposed by the organisation

A grammar does not only say what goes together. It can also say what must not. Simon Willison’s “lethal trifecta” names a dangerous combination: an agent that reads private data, is exposed to untrusted content and can communicate externally (Willison 2025). Each tool may be safe on its own; the danger is in the combination. An organisation should be able to write that down as a rule, excludes, and have it enforced.

This rule does not belong to any server. A vendor publishes its tools; it does not decide what your company forbids. Policy edges belong to the client or the gateway that sits between agents and servers, and they override every other source.

6. A grammar at two levels

A grammar in the linguistic sense does not link specific words. It works on kinds of words: a verb takes an object, an adjective goes before a noun. Specific words that habitually appear together, “strong coffee” rather than “powerful coffee”, are called collocations, and they are learned by use. A tool grammar needs both levels.

Table 1. The two levels of a tool grammar, by analogy with language.
In language For tools Example
parts of speech roles: what kind of thing a tool does approves, pays, converts, notifies, reads private data
grammar rules relations between roles anything that pays requires something that approves
collocations relations between named tools, with weights this payment tool is usually used with that converter (0.71)
a sentence the path of one task approve, convert, pay, post, notify

The two levels fail in opposite ways, which is why both are needed. Collocations are precise for the work an organisation already does, and they say nothing about a tool that was installed yesterday or a workflow nobody has run. Rules over roles carry over to new tools immediately, but they are coarse: they say a payment needs an approval, not which one. A new tool that declares its roles fits into the grammar on the day it appears; use then sharpens the rules into collocations.

MCP already has the beginning of a role system. Tool annotations say whether a tool is read-only, destructive, idempotent or reaches the open world (Model Context Protocol 2025c). These are parts of speech in all but name. The lethal-trifecta rule, for instance, can already be written partly over them: a tool with an open-world hint should not run in the same task as one that reads private data. What is missing is a small shared list of roles beyond those hints, and a way to write rules over them.

6.1 A starting vocabulary

Five relations are a reasonable start. They will not cover everything (conditions such as “if this fails, use the alternative”, or order beyond requires, would come next), but they cover a lot.

Table 2. A proposed starting vocabulary of relations, usable between roles or between named tools.
Relation Meaning Typical source
requires must have run before declared
feeds its output is the other’s input computed
used with often in the same task observed
alternative can replace the other declared
excludes must not run in the same task policy

Each relation can point to a role or to a named tool, and each edge says where it came from so that a reader can weigh it.

6.2 What the protocol needs, and what it does not

What MCP itself would need is small:

  1. A place for relations. Today a convention in _meta, which MCP already allows on tools (Model Context Protocol 2025c); later a field of its own, if the convention proves useful. Tool groups, if adopted, are a natural home for rules that hold inside a group.
  2. A shared vocabulary. A short list of roles, and the five relations above.
  3. Stable names. See below.
  4. A shared way to count use. Whether in MCP or in an existing tracing convention.

The route for such a change exists: MCP evolves through public enhancement proposals, and since December 2025 the protocol is stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation rather than by a single company (Anthropic 2025a). A convention in _meta can be tried first, by a few servers and clients, and proposed once it has shown it is useful.

What it should not include is just as important: any particular way of using the relations. How a client ranks tools, walks the graph or loads a neighbourhood is the client’s business. MCP should carry the grammar, not decide how to read it.

6.3 Edges are local; names are not

Could all of this live in a central registry instead? For composition, I think not. Early web directories sorted pages into folders and were overtaken by search that read the links pages carried themselves (Brin and Page 1998). Links worked because each page published its own and nobody had to hold the map (Fielding 2000). MCP today is a web of pages without links, and each tool should carry its own.

But the web analogy cuts both ways. Links needed no central map, yet they did need a central naming system: a URL is only useful because DNS says what a domain is. The same holds here. An edge to “the convert tool on the fx-rates server” is only meaningful if fx-rates names the same server for everyone, and MCP tool names are unique only within one server; the November 2025 revision added guidance on how to name tools, not a way to name them across servers (Model Context Protocol 2025d). Rules over roles avoid the problem, which is one more reason to prefer them. Edges to named tools across servers need a registry that gives servers stable identities, and the MCP Registry is the obvious candidate (Model Context Protocol 2025a). So the honest position is: relations are local and decentralised; names are not. That is a modest layer, for identity, not a layer that holds the grammar.

7. Borrowing from neural networks

My first idea for this essay was to treat the tool ecosystem as a neural network: tools as neurons, edges as synapses, and a graph neural network (Gilmer et al. 2017) deciding which tools fire for each task. I built one in a small simulation. It worked, but no better than a plain walk along the edges, and it struggled on workflows it had never seen, exactly where rules over roles help. What survived was not the network. It was the principles.

Large neural networks work because they are built on a handful of ideas. Each of them becomes a design rule for a tool grammar:

Table 3. Five principles borrowed from neural networks, and what each means for a tool grammar.
Concept In a neural network As a design rule for tools
Locality a unit only receives messages from its neighbours a tool knows only its neighbours; nobody holds the global map
Sparse activation few units fire for any input (Olshausen and Field 2004; Shazeer et al. 2017) a task loads one neighbourhood, never the catalogue
Plasticity connections that fire together strengthen (Hebb 1949) observed edges strengthen with use and fade without it
Modularity modules are assembled differently for each question (Andreas et al. 2016) clusters that work together become units, across servers
Gating the input decides which paths open the task decides which edges count: a notify edge matters for a payment, not for a report

Sparse activation is the one that pays most directly. Instead of searching a catalogue of thousands, an agent finds one good starting tool by meaning, then loads its neighbourhood: a handful of tools that the grammar says belong with it. Search finds the door; the grammar shows the rooms behind it.

Modularity is where my first intuition about entanglement belongs. Some clusters of tools cannot be understood one at a time: what happens in invoicing tells you a lot about what will happen in currency and mail, whatever the description of any single tool says. Physicists call systems that cannot be described part by part entangled (Horodecki et al. 2009). Nothing quantum happens in a tool catalogue, and the useful mathematics here is ordinary statistics. But the intuition holds. The unit of design is no longer the single tool. It is the group of tools that work together, which can be found from the edges themselves (Newman 2006). Groups and skills are such units, drawn by hand. A grammar lets them emerge from use and cross server boundaries.

8. Who reads the grammar

The strongest argument for relations as data is the one I made for tool descriptions: once something is data, many readers can use it, and most of them need no AI.

  • The language model is the main reader. It does not need a smarter ranking function; it needs the right few tools in its context. Given a tool and its neighbourhood, a model reasons about them far better than it can about a list of thousands. It is also the reader that tolerates an imperfect grammar, which is what makes this attempt different from the last one.
  • A workflow engine can run a path the grammar already knows, with no model at all.
  • A policy gateway can block any call that would complete an excluded pair in the same task.
  • Contract tests can check, on every release, that each feeds edge still type-checks.
  • A catalogue can show people how tools combine, not just what each one does.
  • A small learned router can come later, once the same routing decisions repeat often enough to be worth compiling, as I argued in Fast AI and The Junior Colleague. It is an optimisation, not the paradigm.

9. Objections

“Keep MCP small. Composition belongs to clients and skills.” This is the strongest objection. My answer is that skills and groups prove the need: each skill contains a hand-made grammar, and each group is a set of tools someone decided belong together. But skills are written by one author and live inside one vendor, and groups say nothing about order or data flow. A short list of roles and five relations cost the protocol little. Leaving them out guarantees that every client invents its own version, and none can read the others’.

“This is the semantic web again.” In ambition, yes. In economics, no. The semantic web needed precise descriptions written by people for strict machines. A tool grammar can start from what is free (schemas and observed use), add a little that authors know, and be read by a model that copes with gaps.

“Retrieval trained on use already solves this, with no protocol change.” COLT and Tool2Vec show that learning from use beats matching descriptions (Qu et al. 2024; Moon et al. 2024), and I agree. But what they learn stays inside one retriever: it cannot be shared between clients, checked against schemas, overridden by policy or read by a workflow engine. A grammar does not replace learned retrieval. It gives learned retrieval somewhere to write what it found, and something to start from on the first day.

“Arazzo already does this.” Arazzo describes fixed workflows over OpenAPI operations. MCP tools are not OpenAPI operations, and a fixed workflow does not help an agent build a new one. Arazzo is a good format for the sentences; a grammar is what makes new sentences possible.

“The model can work out complementarity by itself.” Often it can. A model knows that paying in euros may need a currency conversion. It does not know that your company requires approve_invoice before any payment, or that your ledger tool must follow your payment tool. Local conventions are exactly what a grammar records. It also saves the tokens and the time of working them out again on every run.

“Declared edges will be gamed.” Some will. That is why every edge names its source. A client can trust computed and policy edges, discount declared ones from servers it does not know, and let observed weights correct both. A declared edge that nobody ever walks fades.

“Observed edges leak what we do.” They should stay with the client by default. The protocol only needs a common way to count; sharing aggregated weights is a choice, not a requirement.

“Structure will fence the model in.” The strength of the flat catalogue is that a model may draw a path nobody foresaw. A grammar should decide what to show first, not what is allowed, except for the excludes rules an organisation imposes on purpose.

“Edges will go stale.” Tools change. Edges versioned with their tools, computed edges re-checked on every release, and observed weights that decay without use limit the damage. The flat catalogue never goes stale, but it never learns either.

10. What would prove me wrong

  • If context windows and tool search grow faster than catalogues, so that an agent can always read every relevant description, then the grammar adds maintenance and little else.
  • If real tool descriptions carry the complementary signal, so that “pay an invoice” does in practice sit close to “post a ledger entry” in embedding space, then search by meaning would do most of the work. This can be measured on real servers and real traces.
  • If computed edges turn out to be rare or noisy, the cheapest source disappears. This is easy to check: count how many public MCP servers declare output schemas, derive feeds edges from them, and see how many a person would accept.
  • If OpenAPI links stay unused for the same reasons in MCP, the problem is incentives, not the absence of a field, and a field alone will not help.
  • If retrieval trained on use, such as Tool2Vec or COLT, closes the gap that benchmarks like LiveMCPBench measure, without any shared relations, then the grammar’s value shrinks to policy and auditing.
  • If groups, skills and explicit workflows (Arazzo-style) cover the frequent work, the gain from a shared grammar would shrink to the long tail. I suspect the tail is where much of the value is, but that is a hypothesis.

11. Conclusion

MCP got the hardest part right. It turned every tool into a definition that any caller can read. What it left out, for good reasons at first, is how the definitions combine. Today every agent rebuilds that knowledge in its context window and throws it away at the end of the run.

What is missing is not a new central layer and not a trained network. It is a small grammar at two levels: rules about kinds of tools, which hold for tools nobody has used yet, and habits of specific tools, learned from use. Relations can be computed from schemas, declared by servers, observed by clients and imposed by the organisation, and each one should say where it came from. The idea is old; OpenAPI, Arazzo and the semantic web tried parts of it. What is new is a reader that can use a grammar that is cheap, partial and imperfect. The ideas that make neural networks scale tell us how that grammar should behave, and we can borrow them without building a network.

A dictionary lets you look words up. A grammar lets you say something. MCP has the first. The second is what large ecosystems of tools now need.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: The Tool and the Hand
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, October 2026. A short, personal essay. Both figures are schematics of my own, drawn with figs.py; they show a shape, not measured data.

In short. AI raises the ceiling of what one person can do. It does not move the floor each of us stands on. Productivity is not a property of tools but of the relationship between a person and their work: curiosity, ownership, the habit of finishing. A person who postponed before will postpone with AI, only faster. The tool multiplies what is already there, so the gap between people who know why they work and those still waiting to be told will widen. A mindset can change, but through people, not software.

1. The oldest promise

Every new tool arrives with a promise. The printing press would make us wiser. The telephone would bring us closer. The spreadsheet would free the accountant, and the internet would put all knowledge within reach of everyone. Each of these tools delivered something real. None of them delivered the person.

Artificial intelligence arrives carrying the largest promise of all: that anyone, with the right question, can now write, code, analyse and decide faster and better than ever before. And it is true that the ceiling has risen. What has not moved is the floor each of us stands on.

2. The tool amplifies; it does not transform

A tool extends a hand. It does not give that hand an intention. Put a powerful engine in a car whose driver does not know where to go, and you get more horsepower spent idling at the same crossroads.

Productivity is not a property of tools. It is a property of the relationship between a person and their work: curiosity, ownership, the habit of finishing what was started, the courage to show something imperfect and improve it quickly. These are not features you can install.

So the person who used to postpone will now postpone with AI. The one who waited for perfect instructions will now wait for the perfect prompt. The one who avoided hard thinking will find in AI an excellent accomplice for avoiding it, and the result will look polished, which makes it more dangerous, not less. Hesitation, multiplied, is just faster hesitation.

AI multiplies what is already there. It does not supply what is missing.

Meanwhile, the person who was already driven, who asked questions, tried, failed and tried again, will move remarkably further (Figure 1). The real risk of this new tool is not that it replaces people. It is that it quietly widens the gap between those who know why they work and those who are still waiting to be told.

3. A mindset is shaped, not installed

This is not a judgement on the slow. Few people are born indifferent; many were simply never shown another way. Nobody gave them responsibility, nobody trusted them with an unfinished idea, nobody celebrated a small step forward. A mindset is not a fixed trait. It is the sediment of the examples we saw, the feedback we received, and the freedom we were or were not given.

That is why it can change, but not through software. It changes through people (Figure 2). A manager who explains the why before the how. A colleague who shares a half-finished draft without shame. A team where asking a question is a sign of engagement rather than weakness. Small wins, repeated, until finishing becomes a habit and initiative feels natural. This work is slow, human and unglamorous. No licence can buy it, and no rollout plan can schedule it.

4. The question to ask first

Before asking “how do we deploy AI?”, an organisation, or a person, might ask a simpler and more uncomfortable question: what exactly are we about to amplify? If the answer is curiosity, ownership and a taste for doing things well, the tool will be a marvel. If the answer is waiting, fear of being wrong and a lack of purpose, the tool will change nothing except the speed at which we stand still.

The hammer did not build the cathedral. People did: people who knew why they were cutting stone. The tools have never been as powerful as they are today. It has never mattered more to tend to the hand that holds them.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: The Joy of the Question
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Essay, October 2026. All figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py. Figures 3 and 5 use numbers from the studies cited in their captions; the others are schematics.

In short. AI is getting very good at solving problems, and it will keep getting faster. If we measure ourselves by the pace at which we find answers, we have already lost, and it does not matter. The fear is old: Plato already worried that writing would give people the appearance of wisdom without the reality. What remains ours is setting the problems, which asks for creativity, imagination and judgement, and, underneath, caring about them. A machine has no reason of its own to want an answer. We do. Even if the deepest questions stay out of reach for us and for any machine, the motivation to pursue them and the joy of the climb may be what matters most. The risk is that we hand over the effort that builds these things, and children most of all.

TipKey takeaways
  • Solving is being automated fast, but someone still has to say what counts as a good answer, and why it matters. To borrow Nietzsche’s words, the why comes before the how.
  • Losing work can lift us. After superhuman Go programs appeared, professional players made better and more novel moves (Shin et al. 2023).
  • AI evens out execution. What separates people now is judgement: knowing where the tool ends, and when to doubt it (Dell’Acqua et al. 2026; Lee et al. 2025).
  • Effort builds both skill and motivation. Students who practised with a plain chatbot did 17% worse once it was taken away (Bastani et al. 2025). For Spinoza, joy is the feeling of our own power to act growing; a tool that does the climbing for us can take it away.
  • The skills that stay ours are imagination, judgement and the ability to tell information from knowledge. Choosing what is worth our life, and enjoying the pursuit, is not a task to automate.

1. The oldest fear

In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates tells a story. The Egyptian god Theuth brings a new invention to King Thamus: writing. It will make people wiser, he says, and improve their memory. The king is not convinced. Those who rely on it, he answers, will stop exercising their memory, and writing will offer them “the appearance of wisdom, not true wisdom” (Plato, n.d.-b). They will have heard many things without learning them.

Twenty-four centuries later, we have the same conversation about AI. In July 2025, an AI system reached gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad (Luong and Lockhart 2025). A coding agent found a way to multiply two 4×4 complex matrices with 48 multiplications, the first improvement in 56 years on this case (Novikov et al. 2025). By mid-2026, AI systems were settling problems posed by Paul Erdős that had stayed open for decades (Quanta Magazine 2026). The question everyone asks is Thamus’s question: what will this do to us?

The usual answer is a race: how long before the machine is faster than me at my work? I think this is the wrong race. Speed is the machine’s game, and we will lose it. A better question is what we are for, once speed is no longer our job.

Look at how these systems work. To run AlphaEvolve, a person writes down the problem and a program that scores any proposed answer. The machine then searches, far faster than we could. Without that scoring function there is nothing to search for. And behind the scoring function there is something even more human: a reason to care about this problem rather than another.

Nietzsche wrote that whoever has a why to live can bear almost any how (Nietzsche 1889). He was writing about suffering, not software, but the order he gives holds here too. The why comes first, and it gives the how its worth. Figure 1 is how I picture it. In the middle is how: solving. Machines take more of it every year. Around it is which: which problem, and what counts as a good answer. Around that is why: why it matters to us at all. The outer rings are not slower versions of the middle one. They are a different kind of thing.

2. Losing work, gaining height

Thamus was half right. There is an irony here: Plato warned against writing in writing, and that is the only reason the warning reached us. Writing did weaken one kind of memory. But it did not make us less wise; it changed what wisdom asks of us. Freed from memorising, people could compare texts, argue across centuries and build on each other’s work. A century ago, the mathematician Alfred North Whitehead turned this into a rule: “Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them” (Whitehead 1911). Every operation we hand over frees attention for something harder.

Games give us rare evidence, because the quality of a move can be measured. A study of 5.8 million moves by professional Go players between 1950 and 2021 found that after superhuman AI appeared in 2016, human moves became better, and more novel: players began trying moves no one had played before, and those new moves were good (Shin et al. 2023). The study shows an association, not proof of cause, but the timing is striking. The machines did not end the game. The space of the game turned out to be bigger than people had thought, and they went exploring.

This is the hopeful half of my argument: losing much of our work may let us learn more advanced things than we ever had time for. In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes imagined his grandchildren freed from most work, and predicted that humanity would then face “its real, its permanent problem”: how to use that freedom “to live wisely and agreeably and well” (Keynes 1931).

I do not want to make this sound easy. For most people, work is first of all an income, and losing it is not a philosophical opportunity but a threat. How the gains of AI are shared is a real and urgent question, and this essay does not answer it. My subject is narrower: what work means to us, and what we should protect while the rest is decided. Even there, the upper line in Figure 2 does not rise by itself. It rises only for people who keep climbing, and climbing is effort.

3. Knowing where the tool ends

Socrates was called the wisest man in Athens, and he explained why: unlike others, he did not think he knew what he did not know (Plato, n.d.-a). With AI, this old virtue becomes a practical skill.

On execution, AI is a great equaliser. In a call centre with over 5,000 agents, an AI assistant raised productivity by 15% on average, mostly for the least experienced; the best agents gained little (Brynjolfsson et al. 2025). In a creative-writing experiment, the least creative writers gained the most from AI ideas (Doshi and Hauser 2024). Where good answers are known, the tool spreads them.

What it does not spread is judgement about its own limits (Figure 3). In a field experiment with 758 consultants, those using AI on tasks it handles well completed 12.2% more tasks and worked 25.1% faster. On a task chosen to lie just beyond what it could do, they were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the right answer than colleagues without AI (Dell’Acqua et al. 2026). The tool did not say where its competence ended. Knowing that was the person’s job.

Who does that job well? A survey of 319 knowledge workers gives a clue: the more people trusted the AI, the less critical thinking they reported; the more they trusted themselves, the more they reported (Lee et al. 2025). So the difference between people does not disappear. It seems to move, from how well we execute to how well we doubt.

What matters is the loop each of us gets into (Figure 4). In one loop, you ask what matters, the AI explores, you judge, and you come back with a sharper question. In the other, a vague request gets a fluent answer, the answer is accepted, and the next request is no sharper than the last. The first loop is the upper line of Figure 2. The second quietly pulls it down.

4. Effort builds the skill, and the wish

Spinoza gave a definition of joy that I find more useful than any other: joy is our passage from a lesser to a greater perfection, the feeling of our own power to act increasing (Spinoza 1677). In this sense joy is not having the answer. It is becoming able to find it. Which means a tool that hands us the answer can give us the result and take the joy away.

Recent experiments suggest something like this. In four studies with over 3,500 people, working with a generative AI made the work better. But when people then moved to a task on their own, the gain did not carry over, and they reported less intrinsic motivation and more boredom (Wu et al. 2025). Psychology has a name for what was missing. People are moved from the inside when three needs are met: autonomy, the sense of choosing what you do; competence, the sense of getting better at something hard; and relatedness, doing it with and for others (Ryan and Deci 2020). An AI that sets the task and does the hard part can take away the first two without anyone noticing. An AI used to explore questions you chose, on problems you are learning to master, can feed all three.

That is why I worry most about children. An adult who hands a task to AI still has the skill built before. A child who never builds it has nothing to fall back on, and may never discover the pleasure of having worked something out.

The clearest evidence comes from a school in Turkey, where nearly a thousand high-school students practised mathematics with one of two AI tools (Figure 5). With a plain chat assistant, practice grades rose by 48%. With a tutor designed to give hints instead of answers, they rose by 127%. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. Students who had used the plain assistant scored 17% lower than students who never had AI. Students who had used the tutor did about as well as those without AI (Bastani et al. 2025).

Other studies point the same way. University students who revised essays with ChatGPT wrote better essays but learned no more (Fan et al. 2025). Junior developers learning a new library scored 17% lower on what they had learned when AI wrote the code for them, in a study by Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude assistant (Anthropic 2026).

The good news is in the same studies: design matters. A tutor that asks you to try first, and a learner who asks “why?”, keep the effort where it belongs. Spinoza ended his Ethics with a sentence every student could keep: “all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.”

5. Imagination, judgement, and a well-made head

If solving becomes cheap, the skills that matter most are those of the middle ring. Einstein said it plainly. “The formulation of a problem is often more essential than its solution, which may be merely a matter of mathematical or experimental skill,” he wrote with Leopold Infeld; raising new questions “requires creative imagination and marks real advance in science” (Einstein and Infeld 1938).

Psychologists later measured this. In the 1970s, they found that art students who spent more time finding their problem, exploring and changing it before committing, produced more original work and had more successful careers years later (Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi 1976). Donald Schön wrote that professionals do not simply solve the problems given to them: they set them (Schön 1983). What is new is that this is becoming the scarce part. In a large study, research ideas written by a language model were rated more novel than ideas from experts (Si, Yang, et al. 2025). But when 43 researchers spent over 100 hours each carrying the ideas out, the AI ideas lost much more of their score, and their advantage disappeared (Si, Hashimoto, et al. 2025). An idea that sounds new is cheap. Knowing which one is worth months of your life is not.

There is also a trap. When writers used AI-generated ideas, their stories were rated more creative, but they became more similar to each other (Doshi and Hauser 2024). If everyone draws from the same model, the model’s defaults become everyone’s ideas. The creative edge lies in what you bring that the model would not: your experience, your taste, your stubborn questions. When the OECD measured the creative thinking of 15-year-olds for the first time, scores varied widely between education systems: the OECD average was 33 out of 60, and Singapore reached 41 (OECD 2024). That suggests schools make a difference.

Under imagination and judgement lies a more basic skill, and it brings us back to King Thamus: the ability to tell information from knowledge. AI gives us unlimited information, fluent and confident: the appearance of wisdom, in endless supply. None of it is knowledge until someone has done some work on it (Figure 6). Montaigne asked for exactly this in a child’s education more than four centuries ago: better a well-made head than a well-filled one (Montaigne 1580). AI can fill any head at no cost. The making is still ours to do, because the last step, being able to explain and defend something without the tool, happens in a person.

6. What a machine has no reason to want

Now the outer ring of Figure 1, which I believe matters most.

Aristotle opened his Metaphysics with the sentence “all human beings by nature desire to know” (Aristotle, n.d.). Not to possess answers: to know. The desire comes first. A machine works on whatever problem it is given. Whether future machines will ever have something like wishes of their own, nobody knows, and I will not pretend to. But it does not change our side of the question. A result is not valuable in itself. It is valuable to someone: a person with a need, a hope, an idea of how we should live. Deciding what is worth doing is not a technical step; it is a human one.

The philosopher Bernard Suits imagined a utopia like Keynes’s, where machines do all the work. What would people do there? His answer: play games, which he defined as “the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles” (Suits 1978). We climb mountains although helicopters exist. We still play chess, decades after a computer beat the world champion, and millions still play it every day. The obstacle is unnecessary; the climb is the point. When machines can solve a problem, solving it ourselves becomes a choice, and choices are where meaning lives.

Some questions may stay out of reach forever, for us and for any machine: why there is something rather than nothing, what a good life is, what all of this means. Albert Camus wrote about Sisyphus, condemned to push a rock up a hill forever, and concluded that “one must imagine Sisyphus happy” (Camus 1942). The struggle toward the heights, he wrote, is enough to fill a human heart. I do not read this as resignation. I read it as a description of what makes us human: we keep asking, keep climbing, and find joy in it even without a final answer.

A machine may one day reach the top of every hill faster than we can. Being there first is not the same as being glad to be there. That gladness, the motivation to begin, the meaning found on the way, the joy of understanding something for yourself, is not a slower version of what machines do. It is the reason any of it is worth doing.

7. Conclusion

King Thamus feared that a new tool would give us the appearance of wisdom without the reality. He was right that it could; he was wrong that it must. The same is true of AI. On speed, the race is over, and that is fine. What remains is the part that was always ours: choosing which problems are worth our time, judging the answers, and caring about them. AI can help us climb higher than ever, as Go players did, if we keep making the effort. It can also make the climb feel pointless, if we let it take the part that gave us joy.

So for ourselves: write the question before opening the tool, decide what a good answer looks like, and keep doing some things by hand for the pleasure and the skill. For our children: let them try first, teach them to ask “how do you know?”, reward good questions as much as right answers, and leave room for boredom and play, where imagination grows. The machine will find answers. Whether they matter, and the joy of looking for them, is up to us.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: What Survives Comparison
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Evenings with Physics · Part 4 of 4 · Read the whole series

A reader’s question

After Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside, a reader sent me a question I could not stop thinking about:

If two observers inside the same closed universe each keep their own records, do they always end up agreeing on one world?

My first answer was one word: no. That was true, but too short. “No” sounds like the two observers live in different worlds and that is the end of it. What I actually believe fits in one sentence: agreement is always agreement for someone. It exists for whoever holds both records and can compare them. It does not exist anywhere else.

In the last essay one observer came in to rescue the universe from having only one state. This essay puts in two, and follows that sentence through three cases. I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity.

Nobody holds the master copy

The ordinary picture goes like this. There is one world, out there. Each observer takes notes on it. If two observers disagree, at least one made a mistake, and you can find out who by checking against the world.

In a closed universe that last step has nowhere to happen. There is no outside, so there is no referee holding the master copy. The previous essay said that the view from nowhere returns one state, which is to say nothing. So the world cannot be what guarantees agreement. Any agreement has to be produced from inside, by the observers themselves.

That is the real reason for my “no”. Not that observers must disagree, but that nothing is there to make them agree in advance.

The physicists who brought the observer back saw this coming. Harlow, Usatyuk and Zhao also consider two observers: each can treat the other as just more matter, and the rules require the two accounts to fit together. Agreement is not handed out by the universe. It is a condition the rules have to be built to satisfy, and the rules themselves are not settled yet.

Two observers, two pictures

The first way two records can differ came from the last essay. A bigger observer, one that can hold more, sees a richer universe. A smaller one sees a blurrier one.

Lay one record over the other, pixel by pixel, and they disagree almost everywhere. But that is the wrong comparison. The small observer simply did not record the fine detail. On what it did record, the large-scale shapes, the two agree.

So “do they agree?” only has a meaning on the questions both of them can ask. A blurry record and a sharp record do not contradict each other. One is just shorter.

Recent work suggests the differences can go further than blur. In 2024, De Vuyst, Eccles, Höhn and Kirklin showed that in quantum gravity even the entropy of a region, how much it can hide, depends on which observer describes it. Some quantities that looked like properties of the region turn out to belong to the region and the observer together.

When records meet

The second case is where quantum mechanics comes in.

Eugene Wigner imagined it in 1961. A friend sits in a sealed laboratory and measures an electron: up or down. She writes down the result. Wigner stands outside. As long as nothing leaks out, quantum mechanics tells Wigner to describe the whole lab, friend and notebook included, as still in a superposition of “saw up” and “saw down.” The friend has one result. Wigner has a description with both. Two observers, two accounts, and for now neither is wrong.

Since 2018 this has become sharper. Extended versions with two friends and two Wigners show that if every observer treats the others’ conclusions as facts, they reach a contradiction. In 2020 a team led by Kok-Wei Bong tested one such version, called Local Friendliness, in a real experiment. Its conclusion: you cannot keep all of these at once, that observed events are facts for everyone, that no influence travels faster than light, and that experimenters choose their settings freely. The “friends” in that experiment were simple photonic systems, so in 2023 Wiseman, Cavalcanti and Rieffel proposed a version where the friend can reason: an artificial intelligence running on a large quantum computer. Nobody can build it yet.

So quantum mechanics does not promise that one observer’s record is a fact for every other observer. That is the “no” again.

But look at what happens when Wigner opens the door and asks his friend what she saw. Now the two records interact, and quantum mechanics is firm about this case. Measure an electron, measure it again right away: same answer. Ask the friend, and her answer matches her notebook. There is one condition, and it is the heart of the paradoxes: while the lab is sealed, Wigner could in principle undo the friend’s observation, record included. The records whose truth is in doubt are the ones that never meet anything else, or are erased before they can. Records that are kept and brought together agree.

Rovelli’s relational quantum mechanics, which I mentioned last time, makes this a principle. In 2023 Adlam and Rovelli added a rule they call cross-perspective links: when one observer checks another’s record, what they find matches what the other recorded. Consistency is not a property of the world seen from above. It is a rule about meetings. The rule is debated, and so is relational quantum mechanics itself. But whichever view wins, agreement has to come from something that happens between observers.

That is what I meant in my reply. Two observers can tell different stories while apart. When they meet and compare, and their records have survived until then, quantum mechanics makes the stories fit. The agreement exists for them, at the meeting.

Why so many people agree so easily

There is an obvious objection. You and I can both look at the Moon from different continents, never talk, and still agree on where it is. Why does agreement feel automatic?

Wojciech Zurek’s answer is called quantum Darwinism. The Moon is hit by sunlight, and each photon that bounces off carries away a tiny copy of where it is. There are astronomical numbers of these copies: Riedel and Zurek estimated that a speck of dust one micrometre across, in sunlight for one microsecond, has its position copied roughly a hundred million times. You catch some copies; I catch others. We never touch the Moon or each other, but we have read different copies of the same record.

The striking part is how few copies you need. In the toy below, one bit is copied, imperfectly, into sixty small pieces of environment. Read a few percent and you already know the whole bit. Read more and you learn nothing new, until you hold almost all of it. That flat stretch, the plateau, is why the world looks objective: many observers, each with a small and different fraction, land on the same answer.

Zurek chose the word Darwinism on purpose. Only some properties survive being copied over and over without being disturbed, and those become shared, the same for everyone. The rest stay private, or are lost. Parts of this have since been proved in general and seen in the lab, with photons and with spins in diamond. It does not explain why there is one result rather than another, only why everyone sees the same one.

This is very close to the sentence I wrote in my reply before I knew the theory: reality is not what is out there, but what survives comparison. Zurek would say what survives copying. But copying is comparison done in advance, by the environment, on everyone’s behalf. It is still agreement for someone. There are just a great many someones.

Behind each other’s horizons

The third case is the strangest, and it is where my “no” becomes something else.

Our universe is expanding faster and faster, so it has a horizon, a little like a black hole turned inside out. If dark energy stays constant, light that a distant galaxy emits today will never reach us, however long we wait. In empty de Sitter space, the universe from the previous essay, every observer sits at the centre of their own horizon.

Take two observers beyond each other’s horizon, A and C. Neither can ever send the other a message. They can both see light from a shared distant past, so they may hold records of the same old events. But they can never bring those records together.

Do A and C agree on one world? For A and C themselves, the question has no answer. Not an unknown answer: no answer at all. Nothing either of them could ever do would settle it.

The diagram shows one subtlety. A third observer, D, between them, could catch an early message from each and compare them. But D could never tell A or C the result. So agreement between A and C may exist, but only for D. This is the opening sentence in its plainest form.

Physicists have met this before. In 1993 Susskind, Thorlacius and Uglum proposed black hole complementarity: someone who falls in and someone who stays out describe the horizon in incompatible ways, and both are right, because no one can ever hold both accounts. The idea was badly shaken by the firewall argument of 2012 and reshaped by the black-hole information results since 2019. In a form many physicists accept, its core survived: inside and outside are different encodings of the same thing, and no single observer can play them against each other.

In 2025 the same idea reached closed universes. Engelhardt, Gesteau and Harlow applied the new observer rules to a closed universe entangled with a pair of anti-de Sitter universes, the kind holography describes well, and called the result observer complementarity. An outside observer can run a test that says, in effect, there is no closed universe at all. An observer inside has their own consistent description of it. Here there is no D: nobody anywhere can receive messages from both. The result is contested: Antonini and collaborators (2025) and Higginbotham (2026) argued that the outside observer’s test cannot rule the closed universe out. But the debate is the reader’s question, now in the research literature.

So there is a kind of protection. Contradictions are allowed, but only where nobody can catch them.

One world, built

Put the three cases together.

  • Different sizes: their records differ, but on what both can see, they match.
  • When they meet: quantum mechanics makes their records consistent, and the environment often does the meeting for them.
  • Behind each other’s horizons: they can never compare, so for them “do they agree?” has no answer. At most a third observer holds it, and keeps it.

Nowhere in this list does the universe hand out one shared world from the start. One world is not given. It is what records build when they meet. It reaches exactly as far as meetings can reach, and it exists for whoever is at the meeting.

This also fits the grains from the last essay. A grain that pinches off into its own closed universe counts as one state from outside, and is everything to those inside. Now I see why the two descriptions never clash: once the grain has pinched off, nobody inside and nobody outside can ever compare notes, and there is no third place from which anyone could. The horizon that hides the grain also keeps both stories true. I did not know, when I wrote the last essay, that Engelhardt, Gesteau and Harlow had found something very close to this. I find that encouraging, and also a reason to be careful: their result is barely a year old and already disputed.

A short echo in the usual subject

This blog is usually about AI, so one short echo, as an analogy only. Ask two AI models the same question and they may answer differently. There is no master copy of the right answer inside either. What I trust is what survives comparison: answers checked against each other, against a test, against a shared source. Agreement between machines, like agreement between observers, is not stored somewhere. It is built, for someone, where records meet.

The echo also runs the other way. The most demanding Wigner’s friend experiment proposed so far needs a friend that can reason, and the candidate is an AI on a quantum computer. One day “do two observers agree?” may be tested with a machine in the friend’s seat.

What I am not claiming

  • Wigner’s friend, the extended versions (Frauchiger and Renner, 2018) and the Local Friendliness results are about quantum mechanics without gravity. Applying them to observers in a closed universe is my own step.
  • The extended Wigner’s friend results are still argued over. Different interpretations escape the contradiction in different ways; I have described the relational way because it fits these essays, not because it is settled. Relational quantum mechanics itself is under serious criticism.
  • The cross-perspective links rule is a postulate added to relational quantum mechanics, not something derived from it. Lawrence, Markiewicz and Żukowski argue that relative facts are incompatible with quantum theory; Cavalcanti, Di Biagio and Rovelli replied, and the exchange continued in 2025.
  • The rules for including observers in quantum gravity are recent and not unique: Abdalla, Antonini, Iliesiu and Levine proposed different rules, and the two proposals disagree on the number of states. Most of these results use simplified models, often gravity in two dimensions.
  • Black hole complementarity in its 1993 form did not survive the firewall debate unchanged. Among the replies, Harlow and Hayden argued that catching the contradiction would need a computation longer than the black hole’s life; from 2019, Penington and Almheiri, Engelhardt, Marolf and Maxfield showed, mostly in simplified models, how information leaves an evaporating black hole. I use complementarity as an example of the idea, not as established physics. Observer complementarity for closed universes is a 2025 proposal and is contested.
  • Whether our own universe has a permanent horizon depends on how dark energy behaves in the far future. Since 2024 the DESI survey has found hints that it may be weakening; if it fades enough, the horizon could eventually stop being one. The hints are not conclusive.
  • Quantum Darwinism explains why observers agree on an outcome, not why there is one outcome. Its general result (Brandão, Piani and Horodecki, 2015) is about which question observers can ask; agreement on the answer needs the redundancy, which depends on the model. The toy in Figure 2 is a textbook model with perfect symmetry; real environments are messier, though the plateau has been found in more realistic models and in experiments.
  • The connection to the grains is speculation built on speculation.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.
