item.title: Coherence Is Measurable
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
A thought essay, October 2026. This is an argument, not a paper. Figures 1, 3, 4 and 5 are my own schematics. One small experiment backs the central claim: sim.py trains ensembles of ten small neural networks on the handwritten digits that ship with scikit-learn, repeated on ten random train/test splits, in about twelve minutes on a 4-core cloud CPU; results are in results.json and Figure 2 comes from figs.py. The networks are tiny and the task is easy: the experiment tests the shape of an argument, not a language model. Every other claim is cited.

In short. A short passage I came across recently, unsigned, makes a bold claim: the next scientific revolution won’t come from more parameters or larger models; it will come from understanding coherence. I take it as a prompt for thinking, not as a source to cite. As a statement about physics, I can’t test it. As a statement about machine learning, I can, because in AI coherence is not a mystical invariant. It is a family of checks: do the answers agree, does the logic run both ways, does the stated reason match the real one, do two views of the world map to one state. Each check can be measured, used at run time, and trained for. My conclusion: coherence will not replace scale, but it is what we should measure scale by, and a cheap signal for when a model should stop and look. It fails exactly where all the models share the same mistake.

TipKey takeaways
  • Coherence has four working definitions in AI: across samples, across logic, between thought and word, and across views and time.
  • Disagreement is a detector. In my experiment, when ten networks all agreed, they were right 99.8% of the time; most of the errors fell where they disagreed. Published work finds the same for language models (Farquhar et al. 2024).
  • Coherence is a training target. Several recent models are trained to agree with themselves rather than to reproduce every pixel or token (Assran et al. 2025; Song et al. 2023; Irpan et al. 2025).
  • Coherent is not true. When every network learned the same misleading shortcut, agreement no longer told right from wrong: its detection score fell from 0.92 to 0.51, chance level. Withholding the shortcut from part of the training data kept it at 0.73.
  • One rule: probe, measure agreement, answer when coherent, look up or abstain when not, check the coherent answers against the world, and train on what you learn.

1. The claim, read as engineering

In physics, “coherence” has a precise meaning about waves and quantum states. I borrow only the word. In what follows it means agreement: between answers, between directions of a fact, between a model’s reasons and its behaviour, between views of the world.

Read that way, the quote sets coherence against scale. That is a false choice, and the last few years show why. Larger models did become more coherent in measurable ways; for one, the internal representations of different models grow more alike as they scale (Huh et al. 2024). Scale bought coherence.

But scale bought it without measuring it. We trained on next-token loss and discovered coherence afterwards, as a side effect. The better reading of the quote is this: coherence should become a first-class quantity, something we measure, report and optimise directly, not something we hope emerges.

To do that, we need definitions. Figure 1 gives four.

2. Four kinds of coherence

Across samples. Ask a model “Who wrote Middlemarch?” ten times. If it knows, every answer says George Eliot, in different words. If it is guessing, the answers scatter. Self-consistency turns this into a vote: sample several reasoning paths and keep the majority answer, which raised accuracy on maths benchmarks by up to 18 points (Wang et al. 2023). Semantic entropy turns it into an alarm: group the answers by meaning and measure how spread they are; high spread flags likely confabulation (Kuhn et al. 2023; Farquhar et al. 2024). SelfCheckGPT does the same for long text, sentence by sentence (Manakul et al. 2023).

Across logic. A model trained on “Tom Cruise’s mother is Mary Lee Pfeiffer” often cannot answer “Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer’s son?”. This reversal curse holds even for large models (Berglund et al. 2024). More generally, a model’s beliefs should obey simple rules: P(X) and P(not X) should add to one, and paraphrasing a question should not change the answer. Such checks catch errors even when nobody knows the right answer, which makes them useful for evaluating models that may be better than their evaluators (Fluri et al. 2024).

Between thought and word. A chain of thought is only useful if it is the real reason. Often it is not. Models nudged by a hidden bias, such as “the answer is always (A)”, follow the bias and then write a plausible explanation that never mentions it (Turpin et al. 2023). Reasoning models do the same: given a planted hint, they mostly used it without saying so (Chen et al. 2025). Can we read the truth from inside instead? One method finds a direction in a model’s activations that keeps its answers to a statement and to its negation consistent (Burns et al. 2023). But later work showed such probes can lock onto other consistent features, such as a character’s opinion in the prompt, rather than the model’s own knowledge (Farquhar et al. 2023; Levinstein and Herrmann 2024). Interpretability work now traces the internal steps behind an answer more directly (Templeton et al. 2024; Lindsey et al. 2025). Faithfulness is coherence between the inside and the outside, and it is the hardest of the four to measure.

Across views and time. A world model should map two views of the same scene, or two moments of the same motion, to states that fit together. The same may hold across models: networks trained on different data, in different modalities, measure distances between concepts more and more alike as they grow, Huh and colleagues argue (Huh et al. 2024). This is where coherence becomes architecture (section 4).

3. Coherence as a signal, measured

The first use of coherence needs no retraining: measure it at run time and act on it. I tested the idea on the smallest setup I could make honest.

Setup. Ten small neural networks, each trained on a different resampling of 898 handwritten digits, with a different random start; 899 other digits held out for testing. Each network gives one answer. The whole experiment is repeated on ten random train/test splits, and I report the mean, with the spread across splits where it matters. This is an ensemble of independently trained models, not repeated samples from one language model, but the question is the same: does agreement predict correctness? I tested on the clean digits, and on the same digits with heavy pixel noise the networks never saw in training.

Result. Agreement worked as a detector (Figure 2, left):

  • On clean digits, all ten networks agreed on 83% of them, and were right on 99.8% of those. One network alone was right 94.7% of the time; the majority, 97.2%.
  • On noisy digits, a single network dropped to 76.7%. The networks now agreed fully on only 36% of digits, but were still right on 99.6% of those. Agreement fell where the task got hard, which is exactly what a warning signal should do.
  • Agreement separated right from wrong answers with an AUROC of 0.93 on clean digits and 0.88 on noisy ones (spread across splits: ±0.03 and ±0.02).

So agreement ranks answers by trust. The low-agreement ones can go to a lookup, a tool, or an honest “I don’t know”. This matters because today’s training rewards guessing: benchmarks score an abstention like a wrong answer, so models learn to bluff (Kalai et al. 2025). Asking a model how sure it is can help too (Tian et al. 2023), but agreement does not depend on the model’s own sense of confidence.

The cost. Agreement is not free. Ten models, or ten samples, cost up to ten times the compute, and grouping free-text answers by meaning needs a second model to judge which answers say the same thing (Farquhar et al. 2024). For a single digit the vote is trivial; for a paragraph it is not.

4. Coherence as a training target

The second use goes deeper: train for coherence directly.

In vision and world models. A generative model learns by predicting every pixel of the next frame, including leaves, glare and texture that no one could predict. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) predict something else: the representation of the missing part, scored on whether it matches the encoding of the real thing (Assran et al. 2023; Bardes et al. 2024) (Figure 3). V-JEPA 2, trained this way on more than a million hours of video, was adapted with under 62 hours of unlabelled robot video and then planned pick-and-place tasks zero-shot on robot arms in two labs whose data it had never seen (Assran et al. 2025). The loss is not “reproduce the world”; it is “stay consistent with it”.

In generation. Consistency models train a network so that every point along a noisy trajectory maps to the same clean output. That constraint is what allows generation in one or two steps instead of hundreds (Song et al. 2023).

In language models. Consistency training asks a model to behave the same with and without an irrelevant cue: a leading question, a stated opinion, a jailbreak wrapper. Trained this way, models showed less biased reasoning (Chua et al. 2024) and less sycophancy and jailbreak success, whether the consistency was enforced on outputs or on internal activations (Irpan et al. 2025). Nobody had to write the right answer.

The trap. Coherence alone is easy to game. A model that answers “42” to everything is perfectly consistent and useless; a JEPA whose encoder outputs a constant matches its target every time. Every method above therefore needs an anchor. JEPAs use architectural tricks to keep representations from collapsing (Assran et al. 2023); consistency models are tied to real data at the end of the trajectory (Song et al. 2023); consistency training uses the model’s own answer to the clean prompt as the target (Irpan et al. 2025). Coherence is a constraint, not an objective on its own.

5. Where coherence stops

Coherence has a hard limit, and the original quote skips it. Coherent is not true. A conspiracy theory can be perfectly self-consistent. So can a model trained on a stale or biased corpus. Figure 4 makes the point with a simple grid.

The second half of the experiment measures the bottom-left cell (Figure 2, right). I gave every training digit a ten-slot hint naming a digit, like a hint planted in a prompt. The hint was right some fixed share of the time, from 50% to 99%, and named a random digit otherwise. At test time, the hint always named a wrong digit.

  • With a weak hint (right 50% of the time), the networks mostly ignored it: the majority followed the wrong hint on 2% of digits, and agreement still detected errors (AUROC 0.92).
  • As the hint grew more reliable in training, every network learned to lean on it. With a 99% reliable hint, the majority followed the wrong hint on 41% of digits, and agreement could no longer tell right answers from wrong ones: AUROC 0.51 ± 0.02, chance level. Worse, when all ten networks agreed, they were now right only 31% of the time, against 99.7% with the weak hint.
  • A control ensemble trained without hints was unaffected: 97.2% correct with the same wrong hints present. The failure comes from what the networks learned, not from the extra input.

Ten models, ten random starts, ten different resamplings of the data, and they still agreed on the same mistake, because they all learned the same shortcut from the same data. Diversity among models protects against their independent errors, not against what they share.

The shortcut also has a cost when it is not misleading, only useless. Given a random hint, a kind of input they saw in training, networks trained with a 90% reliable hint got 74.6% of digits right, against 94.7% for the control.

One change helped. When the hint was withheld on a random 20% of training digits, every network also had to learn to read the pixels. With the same 99% reliable hint, the majority followed the wrong hint on 18% of digits instead of 41%, and agreement kept an AUROC of 0.73. This is a crude version of the consistency training of section 4: show the model the same input with and without the cue, so it cannot rely on the cue alone. It reduced the blind spot; it did not remove it.

Language models are in a worse position than my ensemble. Repeated samples from one language model share not part of their training but all of it. A shortcut learned in training is therefore largely invisible to the self-consistency checks of section 3: every sample carries it.

Asking the model to check itself does not fix this. Without outside feedback, language models asked to review their own reasoning often change right answers into wrong ones, and overall get worse (Huang et al. 2024).

So coherence is necessary, not sufficient. Internally it removes noise; externally, it must be anchored by retrieval, tools, tests and people. This is the same conclusion as An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle, reached from a different side.

6. A design rule

Put together, the pieces give a loop (Figure 5).

  1. Probe. For any answer that matters, ask more than once: several samples, a paraphrase, the reverse question.
  2. Measure. Score agreement in meaning, not in words. Where you can see inside, check that the stated reason is the one used.
  3. Route. Incoherent: retrieve, call a tool, or abstain. Coherent: answer, and when the stakes are high still check against the world, because shared mistakes look coherent too.
  4. Train. Feed the inconsistencies back as training signal, anchored to clean examples. Same meaning in, same behaviour out.

For small, local models, the loop is especially affordable. Generating a token is limited by reading the weights from memory: about 620 MB for a 4-bit 1B model, and 6,200 MB for a 12B one, as computed in Where Memory Lives. Five samples from the small model read half the bytes of one sample from the large one, and far fewer when the five run as a batch, since a batch reads the weights once. Their agreement then tells you when to reach for the external memory that essay describes.

7. Conclusion

The quote is right about one thing: more parameters alone will not tell us whether a model understands. It overreaches in another: coherence is not a universal invariant waiting to unify reality. In AI it is something humbler and more useful: a set of measurable agreements, between samples, between directions of a fact, between thought and word, between views of the world. Measure them, route on them, train for them, and anchor them in the world, because a mistake every model shares is the one coherence cannot see. That is a research programme, not a revolution, and it can start today.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: Where Memory Lives
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Fast and Local AI · Part 3 of 4 · Read the whole series

An experiment, October 2026. Every number in Experiments 1 to 4 comes from sim.py, plain NumPy on a 4-core cloud CPU, with results in results.json and figures from figs.py. Other people’s numbers are cited where they appear. The networks are deliberately tiny: they test the shape of an argument, not any product. This essay puts to the test two ideas from Fast AI and An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle: bandwidth, and memory outside the weights.

Updated on November 1, 2026. New Section 9: six ideas from Shubham Mahale (processing in memory, analog chips, on-chip SRAM, context compression, editable context, self-organising memory graphs), checked against the experiments.

In short. A language model keeps what it knows in four places: its weights, its working memory (the KV cache), whatever it can look up, and the habits it has compiled. Each is paid for at a different moment, and for a small model on a laptop that decides the design. Four experiments led me to one rule: keep in the weights what is used on every token; look up everything else, and keep what you look up short.

TipKey takeaways
  • Weights are the densest memory, and the most expensive to read. My networks held up to 1.7 bits per parameter, and a model reads all of them for every token.
  • Weights are hard to edit. Fine-tuning on 150 changed or new facts never kept both the edits and the other facts. Rehearsing everything did, after 630,000 training examples. A table needed 150 writes.
  • Looking up is cheap; rereading what you looked up is not. An index searched four million facts in 0.5 ms. But three retrieved passages then cost a 1B model 29 MB on every generated token.
  • Small models hit the working-memory wall first. At 4-bit weights, the cache of Llama 3.2 1B outweighs its weights from about 19,000 tokens.
  • Knowledge has a long tail. Under Zipf’s law, each tenfold increase in facts held answers the same extra slice of questions. Weights cover the head; the tail belongs in a lookup.

1. The question

Debates about small language models usually ask how much of a large model fits on a laptop. That treats a model as one block of knowledge to compress. I think the better question is what should live where?

Generating a token on a laptop is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic: the machine reads every weight, and the whole cache of the conversation, for every token (Alizadeh et al. 2023). So where knowledge lives decides what it costs.

2. Experiment 1: how many facts fit in the weights

Setup. A fact is a key (a random vector of 32 numbers, standing for a question) and a value, one of answers: bits. The memory is a two-layer network,

where:

  • is the key, the 32 numbers that stand for the question;
  • (a table of numbers) and ( numbers) form the first layer, which turns the key into hidden values;
  • keeps the positive hidden values and sets the others to zero;
  • ( numbers) and (256 numbers) form the second layer, which gives one score to each of the 256 possible answers; the highest score is the network’s answer;
  • stands for all of these numbers together, and counts them: in , in , in and 256 in ;
  • , the hidden width, sets the size of the network.

I used : 2,568 to 18,752 parameters. Each network learned facts, offering from half to four times as many bits as it has parameters, in 3,000 full-batch Adam steps, three seeds each. Following Allen-Zhu and Li (Allen-Zhu and Li 2025), I count the bits it holds as

what its prediction knows about each answer beyond a uniform guess, where:

  • is the number of facts, and runs over them;
  • and are the key and the correct answer of fact ;
  • is the probability the network gives to the correct answer;
  • is what a fact is worth: the bits needed to name one answer out of 256;
  • is zero or negative: the bits the network is still missing. Certain of the right answer (), it holds all 8 bits; hesitating between two answers (), it holds 7; guessing blindly (), it holds none;
  • counts a prediction worse than a blind guess as zero rather than negative.

Result. Below capacity, every network kept every bit. Near capacity it peaked at 1.40 bits per parameter for the smallest network, 1.53 for the next, and 1.68 and 1.67 for the two largest, with seeds never more than 0.04 apart. Past capacity it stored less, not more: about 1.4 bits per parameter, with accuracy down to a fifth or a third. Three times more training lifted the peak to 1.80 but barely changed the decline (1.52 to 1.55, 1.45 to 1.49), so the decline is mostly interference between facts, not too little training.

The number is old: Cover showed in 1965 that a perceptron stores about two bits per weight (Cover 1965), and Allen-Zhu and Li measured about two bits per parameter in transformers (Allen-Zhu and Li 2025). Weights are a very dense memory: an 8-bit fact costs about five parameters, under five bytes at 8-bit precision. Quantised to 4 bits after training, the precision most small models run at, their models lost more than half of it.

3. Experiment 2: changing one’s mind

Setup. A network of 18,752 parameters learned 1,500 facts perfectly. Then 75 facts changed and 75 new ones appeared. I updated it in two ways, each over 4 learning rates and 3 training lengths: fine-tuning on the 150 edits only, or rehearsing everything, all 1,575 facts. An external table got the same edits: overwrite 75 rows, add 75.

Result. Fine-tuning on the edits alone never got both right. The runs that learned 97% or more of the edits kept only 28% to 35% of the other facts; the best compromise kept 48% and learned 47%. Rehearsing everything got both to 100%, after 630,000 training examples, a cost that grows with everything the network knows. The table needed 150 writes and 0.04 ms.

Catastrophic interference is not new (McCloskey and Cohen 1989), and editing methods such as ROME and MEMIT do far better than plain fine-tuning (Meng et al. 2022, 2023), though models still degrade as edits accumulate (Gupta et al. 2024). The point is the contrast: in a table, an edit is local by construction; in weights, every fact shares every parameter. Contacts change, prices change, a client asks you to delete their data. A memory you can overwrite row by row is one you can keep true.

4. Experiment 3: looking it up

Setup. I stored ten thousand to four million facts as unit vectors of 256 numbers, clustered around 2,000 topics as real embeddings are. A question is a stored key plus noise, a paraphrase. Exact search compares it with every key, which takes operations: keys of numbers each ( means “grows in proportion to”). An inverted-file index (IVF) groups the keys into clusters once, then compares a question with the cluster centres and with the keys of the nearest clusters only. That takes operations: centres, plus clusters of about keys each. With , both terms grow like , so a memory a hundred times larger costs only ten times more per question (Douze et al. 2024).

Result. Exact search took 29 ms over a million facts and 100 ms over four million. Probing 4 clusters took 0.25 and 0.5 ms, reading 5 and 11 MB. On harder questions, one cluster missed 5% to 20%, while four clusters matched exact search (95.5% against 96% at the noisiest level). My clustered keys flatter any index: on real embeddings, the same recall takes more clusters, and more time.

An external memory is less compact than weights: 1,024 bytes per fact here, or 8 to 64 bytes with compressed codes (Douze et al. 2024), against under five in the weights. But weights are read in full for every token. A lookup reads a few megabytes, only when a question needs it.

What a looked-up fact really costs

In retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020), what the index finds is pasted into the prompt. From then on it sits in the working memory and is reread for every generated token.

Each token of context costs this model 32 KB. Three passages of 300 tokens add 29 MB to every generated token, over five hundred times the search itself. That is still only 5% of the 620 MB of weights, and far less than a model ten times larger, which would read 6,200 MB per token to answer about 11 more points of questions (Section 6). A lookup is cheap only if what it brings back is short: a fact, not three pages.

That is why recent architectures put the lookup inside the model, where a fetched fact never becomes context. Meta’s memory layers read a few rows of a trainable table per token and beat dense models with more than twice the compute, most on factual questions (Berges et al. 2024). DeepSeek’s Engram adds a hashed n-gram table read in constant time (DeepSeek-AI 2026). Gemma 3n keeps per-layer embeddings on local storage (Google 2025).

5. Experiment 4: the working memory

Setup. The KV cache stores a key and a value per token, layer and key-value head:

where:

  • the factor 2 counts one key and one value;
  • is the number of layers (16 in Llama 3.2 1B);
  • is the number of key-value heads per layer (8);
  • is the number of values in each head (64);
  • is the number of bytes per value: 2 at 16 bits, 0.25 at 2 bits.

For Llama 3.2 1B at 16 bits: bytes, 32 KB for every token in the context.

Each new token reads the whole cache and all the weights, so the cache weighs as much as the weights at

where:

  • is the context length, in tokens, at which the two weigh the same;
  • is the number of parameters (1.24 billion for Llama 3.2 1B);
  • is the bytes per weight: 2 at 16 bits, 0.5 at 4 bits;
  • is the bytes per cache value;
  • the top is the size of the weights in bytes; the bottom is the size of the cache for one token.

For Llama 3.2 1B with 4-bit weights and a 16-bit cache: tokens.

I timed one layer shaped like Llama 3.2 1B (Meta 2024) generating a token over caches of 1,000 to 131,000 tokens.

Result. The weights cost 3.6 ms per token at any context. Attention cost 0.3 ms at 1,000 tokens, matched the weights at about 15,000 and took 49 ms at 131,000. By bytes alone the crossover is 59,000; my NumPy attention is slower than a matrix product, so it came earlier.

The formula gives 76,000 tokens for Llama 3.2 1B in 16 bits. Quantise the weights to 4 bits and it falls to 19,000: a long document, or one agent loop with a few tool outputs. For Llama 3.1 70B it is 108,000. Shrinking the weights moves the bottleneck to the working memory. The remedies all keep that memory short: grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023), sliding windows on five of every six layers in Gemma 3 (Gemma Team 2025), 2-bit caches (Liu et al. 2024), which push the 1B crossover back to 151,000, and Cartridges, small caches trained offline that match in-context learning with 38.6 times less memory (Eyuboglu et al. 2026).

6. The arithmetic of the long tail

How much should stay in the weights? Questions are not uniform: models know popular facts far better than rare ones (Kandpal et al. 2023), and retrieval helps most on the rare ones (Mallen et al. 2023). If the -th most asked of facts is asked with probability proportional to (Zipf’s law), a memory holding the most asked answers

where:

  • is the number of facts in the world (a billion in Figure 7);
  • is a fact’s rank by how often it is asked: 1 for the most asked;
  • sets how steep the tail is: with , the classic Zipf’s law, the second fact is asked half as often as the first and the tenth a tenth as often; a larger puts more of the questions on the first few facts;
  • is the number of facts the memory holds, the most asked;
  • adds up the popularity of the first facts;
  • the ratio is the share of all questions that fall on the facts held.

For , , where is the natural logarithm and 0.577 is Euler’s constant. So each tenfold step adds the same share,

where is how much grows when is ten times larger, and for a billion facts. The ratio, , does not depend on : going from a thousand to ten thousand facts adds about 11 points, and so does going from a hundred million to a billion.

A model ten times larger reads ten times more per token for 11 more points. An index ten times larger reads about three times more, once per question. The head belongs in the weights, where it is used constantly; the tail belongs in a lookup. Apple’s hierarchical memories make this split in pretraining: a 160M model fetching 18M parameters from a 4.6B memory bank matched a regular model over twice its size (Pouransari et al. 2026).

7. What it means for small models and Fast AI

  1. Keep in the weights what is used on every token: language, reasoning, tool use, the structure of a domain. Not the price list.
  2. Keep the working memory short: summaries rather than transcripts, a compressed cache, a window.
  3. Look up the long tail, and bring back little: the fact, not the page. Every row can be inspected, corrected and deleted.
  4. Compile what repeats, as in Fast AI: a verified answer, a small tree or an adapter, checked before the model is called.
  5. Consolidate slowly: what is looked up constantly may earn a place in a habit; what is wrong is deleted, in one line, not one training run.

Agent memory systems are building the top of this stack: MemGPT, now Letta, pages context like an operating system (Packer et al. 2023); Mem0 and A-MEM extract and link memories across sessions (Chhikara et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2025); Titans learns a memory at test time (Behrouz et al. 2024). A small model has the least room in its weights and the least bandwidth to spare, so it gains the most from putting each memory in the right place.

8. Recent work, with code

Table 1. Recent work on the four memories. Code links checked on 25 October 2026. Benchmarks of agent memory systems are still young, and the vendors’ own scores often disagree with independent ones; I would compare them on your own data.
Work Memory it addresses Idea Code
Physics of Language Models 3.3 (Allen-Zhu and Li 2025) Weights About 2 bits of knowledge per parameter —
Memory Layers at Scale (Berges et al. 2024) Weights, sparse Trainable key-value lookup inside the model facebookresearch/memory
Engram (DeepSeek-AI 2026) Weights, sparse Hashed n-gram memory, constant-time lookup deepseek-ai/Engram
Hierarchical memories (Pouransari et al. 2026) Weights + bank Small model, long-tail facts in a fetched memory bank —
Titans (Behrouz et al. 2024) Learned at test time A neural memory updated during inference lucidrains/titans-pytorch (unofficial)
KIVI (Liu et al. 2024) Working memory 2-bit KV cache, no fine-tuning jy-yuan/KIVI
Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al. 2026) Working memory A small cache trained offline per corpus HazyResearch/cartridges
LLM in a Flash (Alizadeh et al. 2023) Weights on flash Load only the weights a token needs —
Faiss (Douze et al. 2024) External Vector indexes, IVF and beyond facebookresearch/faiss
MemGPT / Letta (Packer et al. 2023) External, agent The context as virtual memory letta-ai/letta
Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025) External, agent Extract and update memories across sessions mem0ai/mem0
A-MEM (Xu et al. 2025) External, agent Linked notes that reorganise themselves agiresearch/A-mem
llama.cpp All, locally Quantised weights and KV cache on a laptop ggml-org/llama.cpp

9. Six ideas from Shubham Mahale

After this essay came out, Shubham Mahale sent me six technologies that, in his view, solve the memory problem. They deserve a careful answer, because each one attacks one of the four memories, and each changes a price measured above. I take them one at a time: what is right, what I would challenge, and what it does to the rule.

1. Processing in memory. Build the arithmetic inside the RAM, so data never has to travel. This aims at the right target. Experiments 3 and 4 showed that generating a token is mostly a matter of reading bytes, and processing in memory attacks exactly that. It exists: Samsung built small compute units into HBM2 memory and ran unmodified applications on it (Lee et al. 2021). AttAcc puts the attention over the KV cache there, because attention reads many bytes for each operation whatever the batch size (Park et al. 2024).

What I would challenge is “never”. The data still moves, from the memory cells to small units next to the banks. These units are simple, and they suit the matrix-vector work of generating one token better than everything else. And, as far as I know, they are not yet in the laptops this essay is about. Still, this is the one idea that could change my conclusion. If reading weights becomes much cheaper, a fact in the weights costs less, and the line between weights and lookup moves toward the weights. It does not change Experiment 2: a fact stored in weights is just as hard to edit, wherever the arithmetic happens.

2. Analog chips with memristors. Freeze the weights into analog circuits and compute at the speed of electricity. Here a weight is a conductance, a multiplication is Ohm’s law and a sum is Kirchhoff’s. It works: IBM’s analog chip, with 35 million phase-change memory devices, matched software accuracy on keyword spotting and came close on a larger speech model, at up to 12.4 trillion operations per second per watt (Ambrogio et al. 2023). Phase-change memory is a close cousin of the memristor. (“Neuromorphic” usually means something else: chips that compute with spikes.)

I would challenge “the speed of electricity”. The gain is energy, because the weights never leave the array. The limits are elsewhere: converters between analog and digital, limited precision, and drift over time. The word “freeze” matters even more. Rewriting an analog weight is slower and less precise than writing a row in a table, and the larger model needed about three devices per weight, 45 million weights on 140 million devices. Analog weights are the extreme case of Experiment 2: ideal for what never changes, such as language and reasoning, and the worst place for a price list. This strengthens the rule rather than replacing it.

3. On-chip SRAM in NPUs. Keep the conversation context on the die. SRAM is fast and sits next to the arithmetic, so this works for what fits. The question is what fits. Llama 3.2 1B needs 32 KB of cache per token at 16 bits (Section 5). A generous 64 MB of SRAM holds 2,000 tokens, or 16,000 with a 2-bit cache. That is a conversation, not a document. SRAM rewards a short working memory; it does not replace keeping it short.

4. Context compression. A tiny model squeezes the text before the main model reads it. This attacks the cost in Figure 5 directly, the 29 MB that retrieved passages add to every token. LLMLingua drops the tokens that a small model judges unimportant, up to 20 times, with a small loss on its benchmarks (Jiang et al. 2023). Gist tokens and the in-context autoencoder learn compact representations instead (Mu et al. 2023; Ge et al. 2024). Cartridges, in Section 5, do it offline.

I would challenge two things. First, compression loses information, and it loses first what a small model judges unimportant: rare names and exact numbers, which is the long tail the lookup was there for. Second, “keeping massive contexts stable” is a claim to measure on your own data, not an assumption. I would compress after the lookup, not instead of it. Fetch the fact, not the page, and there is little left to compress.

5. Editable context. The model edits, prunes and rewrites its own memory, like a live file. I agree. This is point 2 of Section 7, and MemGPT, now Letta, and Mem0 already do it (Packer et al. 2023; Chhikara et al. 2025). What I would add is a guard. A model rewriting its own notes makes a summary of a summary. Each pass can drop or bend a fact, and nobody sees it happen. Keep the originals in the external memory, with their source, so that any summary can be checked and redone.

6. Self-organising memory graphs. Reinforcement learning turns the external memory into a knowledge graph that reorganises itself around what the AI forgets. This exists too. A-MEM links notes and updates them as new ones arrive (Xu et al. 2025). Zep keeps a knowledge graph that records when each fact was true (Rasmussen et al. 2025). Memory-R1 uses reinforcement learning to train a manager that chooses, for each new fact, to add, update, delete or do nothing, and it learned this from 152 question-answer pairs (Yan et al. 2025).

I would challenge what the learning optimises. The reward is answering benchmark questions, not being true and not honouring a request to delete. A memory that reorganises itself is also harder to inspect, and inspecting, correcting and deleting were the reasons to keep memory outside the weights in the first place (Section 3). A graph walk also costs more than one index probe. I would let a learned policy propose changes, and keep the store itself plain, versioned and deletable.

Table 2. Six ideas from Shubham Mahale, placed among the four memories.
Idea Memory it acts on What it changes My verdict
Processing in memory Weights, cache Cheaper reading of every byte Real; could move the line toward the weights
Analog chips Weights Energy; weights stay in place Strengthens the rule: frozen means hard to edit
On-chip SRAM Working memory Fast cache, if it fits Rewards a short context; does not replace it
Context compression Working memory Fewer bytes per token Useful after a lookup; loses the long tail first
Editable context Working memory Bounded context Agree; keep the originals
Self-organising graphs External memory Better organised lookup Keep the store inspectable and deletable

The six ideas sort neatly into the four memories: three are hardware that lowers the price of reading, three are software that keeps the working memory short and the lookup organised. Hardware changes the prices in Figures 5 and 6. It does not change the arithmetic of editing in Experiment 2, nor that of the long tail in Section 6. If processing in memory makes reading weights nearly free, the line moves toward the weights. It moves; it does not disappear. A fact you must be able to correct or delete still belongs in a row, not in a parameter.

10. What this experiment does not show

  • My facts are random. Real knowledge has structure a model can compress, so weights may do better than my networks.
  • My networks are tiny: two layers, at most 19,000 parameters.
  • My questions are synthetic. Real retrieval must embed a question first; it can miss, or find the fact and see the model ignore it.
  • Plain fine-tuning is the weakest editor. Better methods narrow the gap, but still edit weights that every fact shares.
  • NumPy is not a serving engine, which is why Figure 6 also gives the byte count.
  • Zipf is a model. A specialist’s questions may have a shorter tail, which argues for specialists.

11. Conclusion

We say a model knows something as if knowledge lived in one place. It lives in four, at four prices: dense weights read on every token, a working memory that grows with every token, a bulky but cheap and correctable lookup, and habits that cost almost nothing once built. Large models can afford to blur them. Small ones cannot, and that is their advantage. Keep in the weights what is used on every token, keep the working memory short, look up the long tail, compile what repeats.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

item.title: Work Has Mass
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
An outsider’s view. I know Scrum from years of practice; SAFe I know only from its public framework, and practitioners will know where real trains differ. The physics is a metaphor, used on purpose; the numbers come from a toy model described in full. Figures are my own, made with figs.py. This essay follows the Agentic Coding series, which looked at the code; here I look at the organisation around it.

TipThree laws of work mass
  1. Everything you make, you carry.
  2. AI lowers the cost of making, not of carrying.
  3. A process is mass too. In a heavier universe, frameworks must get lighter.

The wrong debate

Conversations about AI and agile frameworks fall into two camps. One says AI makes Scrum and SAFe obsolete: if an agent builds a feature in an afternoon, why plan in two-week sprints, or in ten-week increments with a hundred people in a room? The other says nothing changes: AI is just a faster tool inside a good process.

Both camps look at production: how fast work is made. But the frameworks were never only about production. They are about how a group of people carries a growing body of work over time without losing control of it. What should change them is not what AI makes, but what it leaves behind. And the answer, I will argue, is not more framework. It is less.

Every item has mass

Every item that enters the system stays for a while, and some stay for good: a story, a pull request, a feature, a test, a document, a dependency, an open decision, a backlog item someone will “get to later”. Each needs attention to keep: someone must understand it, maintain it, answer questions about it, or at least remember it is there.

I call that ongoing cost the item’s mass. Mass is not value. A small feature used by thousands can be light; a generated module nobody fully understands can be heavy.

In general relativity, mass curves spacetime: objects near a large mass follow curved paths, and time runs slower for them. That is a good picture of what accumulated work does to a team:

  • Paths bend. A new request is pulled toward the heavy parts of the system: the legacy module, the integration everyone depends on, the decision nobody has made.
  • Time slows near mass. The same change takes longer in a heavy system, because each step must account for more of what already exists.
  • There is a horizon. If mass keeps growing, all the team’s attention ends up carrying what exists. Requests still go in. Nothing comes out.

None of this is new. Lehman stated it as a law of software evolution: complexity grows unless work is spent to reduce it (Lehman 1980). Lean calls unfinished work inventory (Reinertsen 2009). Brooks showed that communication paths grow faster than headcount (Brooks 1975). What is new is the rate.

What AI changes: the cost of creating mass

AI makes producing an item much cheaper. It does not, or not yet, make carrying it much cheaper. Someone still has to decide whether a feature should exist, understand how it fits, own it when it breaks, and remember why it was built. As a balance:

where is the mass of the system, the team’s total attention and the attention one unit of mass needs. Production has become cheap; removal was rarely planned at all. So grows faster, and shrinks faster.

The smallest model I could build: a team has 100 hours of attention per sprint. The system starts with 250 items needing 0.1 hours each, so a quarter of the team already carries the past. A new item takes 6 hours to produce by hand or 1.5 with AI, plus 3 hours to absorb (review, decide, integrate). Whatever is left after carrying goes into new items, and every new item stays. These assumptions do most of the work; I return to them in the objections.

  • By hand, the team delivers 8.3 items in the first sprint and 6.3 in the last; carrying grows from 25% to 44% of its attention.
  • With AI, it delivers 16.7 items in the first sprint, and every dashboard looks wonderful. By the end of the year it delivers 9.5, with 58% of its attention on carrying. In the second year the gain is almost gone: 5.3 items per sprint against 4.7 by hand.
  • With AI and a mass budget, whenever carrying would exceed 35% of attention, the team removes items (deletes code, retires features, closes backlog items) before adding new ones. It delivers 13 items per sprint, in the first year and the second.

Over the first year the budget buys little: 356 items against 332, about 7% more. What differs is where each team stands at the end: one delivers 13 items a sprint with a third of its attention on the past, the other 9.5 and falling, with almost 60% on the past. AI does not change the shape of the problem, only its speed. A system that took a decade to become heavy can now do it in a year, and our frameworks were tuned, implicitly, for the decade.

Time dilation

Lead time depends on spare capacity. Queueing theory has known for sixty years that as load approaches capacity, waiting time does not grow steadily; it explodes (Kingman 1961; Little 1961). Mass eats spare capacity. Figure 3 adds one assumption to the model: requests arrive at a steady rate that needs 35% of the team.

This is consistent with what teams report: we produce more than ever, and everything takes longer. In 2024, DORA found more AI adoption associated with slightly lower delivery throughput (about 1.5%) and stability (about 7.2%) (DORA, Google Cloud 2024). In 2025, throughput turned positive but stability stayed negative, and the authors’ explanation is close to this essay’s: change volume outruns the controls downstream, and teams in tightly coupled systems see little or no benefit (DORA, Google Cloud 2025). Experienced developers were even found slower with early-2025 tools in their own large, mature repositories (Becker et al. 2025). None of these studies measured mass, but all point the same way: the gain from faster making is smallest where there is most to carry.

Measuring mass

Mass does not need to be precise to be seen. Two numbers are enough to start.

  • The carrying share. Tag every ticket, or every hour, as new or carry. Carry is everything spent on what already exists: support, incidents, upgrades, questions, reviews of changes that touch it. This is the x-axis of Figure 3.
  • The heaviest items. Once a quarter, attribute the carry hours to the items that caused them and list the top ten. Mass is very unequal; a few services, integrations or open decisions usually carry most of it. That list is where removal starts.

A framework is mass too

The third law is the one I find most important. Every event, role, artifact, metric and tool in a framework is an item in the system, and costs attention every sprint whether or not it helps. Frameworks grow by addition, and almost nothing is removed. When AI makes the work heavier, a heavier process is the last thing the system needs. So I would apply one test to every element of Scrum and SAFe:

The mass test. Does this element remove or prevent more mass than it adds?

My placements matter less than the pattern. The parts that say no pass. The parts that count fail. A Sprint Goal, a Definition of Done, a review, an iteration reserved for removal: each decides what not to carry, and costs little. Estimating every item, refining a long backlog, synchronising a large train: each manages a quantity of work, and quantity is exactly what AI has made cheap. Some elements sit in between and can be slimmed rather than cut. PI Planning is the clearest case, and SAFe is already moving it: its AI-Native guidance replaces the two-day event with a one-day PI Outcome Planning, and folds the System Demo and Inspect and Adapt into a two-hour event each iteration (Scaled Agile, Inc. 2026). Applied honestly, the test does not reject either framework. It shrinks both to their core.

Scrum: lighter, not looser

The Scrum Guide is already short: empiricism and lean thinking, a team of ten or fewer, a time-box of one month or less, five events and three commitments, the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done (Schwaber and Sutherland 2020). It says nothing about story points or velocity; those are common add-ons, and most of what makes Scrum heavy in practice lives in the add-ons.

Table 1. Scrum, read again with mass in mind. The middle column is my reading of the Scrum Guide and of common practice; the right column is my proposal.
Element Calibrated for In a heavier universe
Sprint A rhythm to produce a usable increment A rhythm to absorb one: decide, integrate, understand.
Sprint Goal Focus for the sprint Keep. The cheapest way to say no.
Definition of Done The quality an increment must meet Keep, and add: what it costs to carry, what was removed to make room.
Product Backlog An ordered list, refined as needed Short, with items that expire. AI can fill it without limit.
Sprint Review Inspect the increment Inspect the increment and the mass ledger (Figure 6).
Daily Scrum Daily inspection toward the goal Keep it short, or async for a small team.
Story points, velocity (add-ons, not in the Guide) How much the team can make Drop. With AI they measure mass added. Use lead time and the carrying share.
Team size Ten or fewer, to keep communication manageable The limit is the mass each person carries. Five people with AI can carry the mass of twenty.

The backlog needs evaporation. When writing a backlog item took effort, the effort was a filter. Now an AI can turn every meeting into ten well-written stories, and every story is a promise with mass. Untouched for three sprints, an item expires unless someone renews it. Black holes slowly evaporate. Backlogs should too.

What remains is Scrum at its core: a goal, a standard, a short list, a rhythm of inspection, and a ledger of what the team carries. Less framework than most teams run today, not more.

SAFe: smaller trains, fewer layers

SAFe’s central structure is the Agile Release Train (ART), a long-lived team of agile teams, generally 50 to 125 people (Scaled Agile, Inc. 2023), that plans together every 8 to 12 weeks (Scaled Agile, Inc., n.d.-b). Work is ranked with Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF): cost of delay divided by job size, an idea from product development flow (Reinertsen 2009).

SAFe already knows that existing work has weight. At each interval boundary, trains agree on a capacity allocation: the share of capacity for new features against enablers, technical debt and maintenance (Scaled Agile, Inc., n.d.-a). That is close to a mass budget, and trains that use it well are ahead. The difference is what is limited. A capacity allocation caps the effort spent on old work; a mass budget caps the old work itself, and forces removal when it grows.

WSJF stops discriminating

With AI, job sizes shrink, but unevenly: small features hit a floor, complex ones shrink less. The denominator loses its spread, and the ranking collapses toward cost of delay alone. And job size never measured what a feature costs to carry, which is now the larger part.

The fix is small: add the carrying cost to the denominator,

where carrying cost is a relative estimate of the attention the feature will need in its first year. A chat assistant is quick to build and slow to carry, so it falls; a faster search adds almost nothing to carry, so it rises. And it is enough to score the top of the backlog: ranking features that will never be built is itself mass.

Smaller trains, fewer layers

50 to 125 people is a coordination limit, learned from teams who produced at human speed. But a train does not coordinate people; it coordinates what they produce and must keep consistent: interfaces, dependencies, shared data, shared decisions. If each person adds three times more mass, a train reaches that limit at about a third of the size.

The tempting answer is more structure. The mass test points the other way. Split trains by mass, long before 125 people, so that each carries less. Smaller trains need fewer sync meetings and fewer coordinating roles, and may need less of the structure above them. Planning shrinks with them: each team brings a mass budget next to its capacity, the board shows only the dependencies that cross teams, and the Innovation and Planning iteration becomes the home of removal. SAFe with AI should look less like a bigger SAFe and more like a few small, light trains, each with a clear budget of what it is allowed to carry.

What I would actually do

  1. Measure the carrying share and list the ten heaviest items.
  2. Set a mass budget, and treat crossing it like a red build: stop adding, start removing.
  3. Make removal a deliverable, shown at the Sprint Review and System Demo next to what was added.
  4. Let items expire: backlog items, open questions, generated documents.
  5. Price mass into priority: WSJF with carrying cost, for the top of the backlog only.
  6. Size teams and trains by mass, not headcount.
  7. Put the framework through the mass test, these seven proposals included.

That last point matters, because these are new practices and an essay against framework mass should not quietly add some. Each one replaces something heavier. The carrying share and lead time replace story points and velocity. Expiry replaces the refinement of a long backlog. The ledger replaces a status report, and is one chart in a review that already exists. The mass budget is a number in a planning event that already exists, not a new event. If one of them does not remove more than it adds in your team, drop it.

Objections

“This is technical debt, or Lean inventory, with a new name.” Partly. But a well-built feature that people use is neither debt nor inventory, and it must still be carried. Lean’s inventory is mostly unfinished work; the mass that grows fastest with AI is finished work. Lean also says to manage a system at its constraint (Goldratt and Cox 1984), and the constraint has moved from making to carrying.

“AI will carry the mass too.” In part, yes: agents already read code and summarise documents, which lowers . If falls as fast as production costs, this essay is wrong. I doubt it will, because the mass that matters most needs a person: accountability for a feature, the decision to keep or kill it, the customer who depends on it.

“Nobody gets promoted for deleting things.” True, and the strongest reason a mass budget may fail. Organisations reward what is added. That is why removal must be shown and counted at the same events as delivery, and why the ledger has two columns. What is not seen is not rewarded.

“The model is too simple.” It is: one team, constant parameters, items that never get lighter, and an AI that lowers the cost of making but not of carrying. The model shows the consequence of those assumptions, not their truth. If a better one shows mass levelling off on its own, I would like to see it.

“The physics is decoration.” Perhaps. But metaphors choose what we look at. Velocity made teams look at speed. Mass would make them look at what speed leaves behind.

Conclusion

Scrum and SAFe are not wrong. Empiricism, short feedback loops, small teams, shared cadence and economic prioritisation are as useful with AI as without it. But both were calibrated in a universe where producing work was the hard part, and where mass grew slowly enough to be someone else’s problem later.

AI has changed the rate at which we create mass, not yet the rate at which we carry it. The reflex will be to add: more ceremonies to control more output, more roles to coordinate more teams, more layers to plan more work. That adds mass to a system already falling into its own well. The better answer is the opposite: measure the mass, budget it, price it, remove it as deliberately as we add, and then put the frameworks themselves on the scale.

Everything you make, you carry. In a heavier universe, start by carrying less framework.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

item.title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
item.dc:creator: Stéphane Cuenat
item.description:
Evenings with Physics · Part 3 of 4 · Read the whole series

Continued in What Survives Comparison, which asks what happens with two observers instead of one.

Two ideas that would not stay apart

In A Universe Without a Bottom I left two thoughts side by side. The first: maybe nothing creates everything. The second: maybe there are grains inside grains, with no final layer.

I treated them as separate questions. A few days later they started to look like one question. And the black hole formula, which I thought said there must be a floor, turned out to say something stranger.

I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity. But I think I asked the earlier questions slightly wrong.

Nothing is not empty

In the last essay I called infinite temperature “the closest thing to nothing.” Every possibility equally likely. No preference, no structure.

That was half wrong. A state where every possibility is equally likely is not a state with zero information. It is the state with the most possibilities: maximum entropy. You cannot tell the possibilities apart, but they are all there.

This matters because of where the model points. For several years Susskind has argued that this exact system, at infinite temperature, describes de Sitter space: a universe with nothing in it except a horizon around the observer. An empty universe like this carries the largest entropy any region can have. Its horizon is covered with tiles, just like a black hole.

So the two images in my first essay may be the same image. “Nothing” and “a surface that knows everything” could be one thing, seen from different sides.

A universe with one state

Then I found a result that seemed to say the opposite.

Some universes are closed: travel in a straight line long enough and you come back to where you started. Our universe might be one of them. Over the last few years several groups calculated how many different states such a universe can be in, using the newest tools of quantum gravity. The answer kept coming out the same: one.

One state. Not a large number, not a small number. One. The whole universe, stars and galaxies included, would carry less information than a single coin toss. There is nothing to choose between, so there is nothing to know.

The physicists themselves did not like this. Our universe clearly has more than one possibility in it. I am writing this sentence and not another one. So what went wrong?

Someone has to be inside

The answer proposed by Harlow, Usatyuk and Zhao is simple to say. The calculation forgot the observer.

It described the universe as if from outside. But a closed universe has no outside. Nobody can stand there and look at it. The philosopher Thomas Nagel called the dream of perfectly objective knowledge the view from nowhere: the world seen from no particular place. Here the view from nowhere is not just hard to reach. It returns nothing.

So put an observer inside, treat the edge of that observer as a kind of boundary, and the many possibilities come back.

One warning, because the word is dangerous. “Observer” here does not mean a mind, a consciousness or a person. In these calculations an observer is any physical system with a limited number of internal states that can keep a record. A clock would do. A detector would do. Nothing mystical is happening. What changes is that there is now a reference point.

There is a catch, and I find it beautiful. How much of the universe the observer can describe depends on how much the observer can hold. A bigger observer, with more internal states, sees a richer and more accurate universe. A tiny one sees a blurry one.

So the information in the universe is not simply “out there.” It exists between the universe and something inside it. This is close to an idea Carlo Rovelli proposed in 1996, relational quantum mechanics: physical properties are not owned by things, they exist only relative to other things. The new calculations do not prove this view. But they point the same way.

Two kinds of nothing

Now put the two results next to each other.

  • No observer: one state. Zero alternatives. Nothing to know.
  • One observer at the centre: a horizon full of tiles. Every alternative equally likely. Everything possible, nothing distinguishable.

Both look featureless. Both feel like “nothing.” But they are featureless for opposite reasons. The first has no possibilities. The second has all of them, and no way to tell them apart.

Here is my step. Maybe these are not two different universes. Maybe they are the same universe, once without a reference point and once with one. Without one, the universe is nothing. With one, it is everything its horizon can hold.

This is less of a leap than I first thought. De Sitter space, taken as a whole, is itself a closed universe, so the one-state result should apply to it too. And in 2022, Chandrasekaran, Longo, Penington and Witten showed that the entropy of a de Sitter horizon only becomes well defined once an observer is included, and that empty de Sitter space is then the state of maximum entropy. As far as I know, nobody has put these results together in exactly this way. But the pieces fit.

Philosophers got here long before the equations. Hegel opened his Science of Logic (1812) with this very puzzle: pure being, with no determination at all, cannot be told apart from pure nothing. What sets things in motion, for Hegel, is becoming, the passage between the two. Two centuries later, physics seems to add one thing. What turns nothing into everything is a point of view.

Grains again

In the first essay I was stuck on a contradiction. History suggests the layers never end. The black hole formula says a region can hold only a limited amount of information, so it cannot hide infinite layers. There must be a floor.

Remember the 1987 bubble: a tiny pocket of dense energy that grows into a new universe. From outside it looks like a small black hole that disappears. From inside it is a whole cosmos.

Physicists have known for a long time that this is uncomfortable. A small black hole should hold only a little information. How can a whole universe fit inside? Wheeler called this kind of object a “bag of gold.”

The one-state result changes the question. At first, seen from outside, the bubble is a small black hole, and that black hole does carry some information on its surface. But the bubble then pinches off and becomes a separate closed universe. From that moment, with nothing of ours inside it, it counts as one state. It costs us almost nothing. From the inside, with its own observers, it is everything.

And the same flip can repeat:

  • Inside that grain, a new bubble forms. To the grain, it counts as one state. To its own inhabitants, it is a cosmos.
  • Our universe might be a grain in someone else’s. To them, we would be one state. To us, we are everything.

Leibniz imagined something like this three centuries ago. In his Monadology (1714) he wrote that each portion of matter is like a garden full of plants, and that each branch of every plant is again such a garden. He also said that his ultimate units, the monads, “have no windows”: nothing comes in, nothing goes out. A grain that counts as one state from outside is a monad without windows.

Pascal, whose fear of infinite spaces I quoted last time, wrote in the same Pensées that we stand between two infinities, the infinitely large and the infinitely small, unable to see either end. He took this as a limit of human sight. Perhaps it is more than that. Perhaps each end is hidden by construction, from wherever anyone stands.

The contradiction disappears. Each level has a floor, but only for whoever counts from outside. The chain can go on forever because each grain is almost invisible to the one around it. The black hole formula does not forbid infinite layers. It only forbids seeing them.

Where information begins

I ended the first essay with “from nothing to nothing,” and the hope that the middle still matters. I would now say it differently.

Not from nothing to nothing. Nothing from outside, everything from inside, at every level, with no last level.

That makes my earlier ending more literal. If a universe has only one state until something inside it can keep a record, then the middle is not just where meaning lives. It is where information starts to exist. Not because anyone is conscious, but because something is somewhere.

This brings the question back to the usual subject of this blog. A large language model has a strangely similar shape. Before you ask it anything, it holds an enormous space of possible answers, all weighted, none chosen. Seen from outside, it is a horizon of possibilities with nothing in particular in it. An answer appears only when a question arrives from a particular place. Asking is not reading out something already written down. It is the moment the possibilities narrow into one.

This is an analogy, not physics. I already took the first essay’s question to an image generator in Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary. But the lesson may be the same at both scales. Information is not stored somewhere, waiting. It happens at the boundary between a system and whatever stands inside it, or in front of it.

I started by believing the universe must be simple. Maybe it is. From outside, it is as simple as anything can be: one state. The complexity is a view from inside. And we are inside.

What I am not claiming

  • The one-state result comes mostly from simplified models, often with gravity in two dimensions. Physicists find it fairly convincing, but it is not settled for our universe.
  • Linking it to the de Sitter results is my own reading. As far as I know, none of the papers below states it this way.
  • Whether a 1987-style bubble really becomes a closed universe in the sense of these calculations is an open question.
  • The idea that the nesting never ends is speculation, not a result.
  • Hegel, Leibniz, Pascal and the comparison with AI are echoes, not evidence. They show the idea is old, not that it is true.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

Sources

  • Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind, Holograms and Standard Models (2026)
  • Leonard Susskind, De Sitter Space has no Chords. Almost Everything is Confined (2023)
  • Daniel Harlow, Mykhaylo Usatyuk and Ying Zhao, Quantum mechanics and observers for gravity in a closed universe, JHEP (2026)
  • Quanta Magazine, Cosmic Paradox Reveals the Awful Consequence of an Observer-Free Universe (2025)
  • Chandrasekaran, Longo, Penington and Witten, An algebra of observables for de Sitter space, JHEP (2023)
  • Blau, Guendelman and Guth, “Dynamics of false-vacuum bubbles”, Physical Review D 35, 1747 (1987)
  • Carlo Rovelli, Relational quantum mechanics, International Journal of Theoretical Physics 35 (1996)
  • Thomas Nagel, The View from Nowhere (1986)
  • G. W. F. Hegel, Science of Logic, Book One (1812)
  • G. W. Leibniz, Monadology (1714), §7 and §67
  • Blaise Pascal, Pensées (1670), on the two infinities

The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.
